units.title: From amino acid to protein
units.subtitle: Follow a side chain from its chemistry to a protein’s behavior.

blocks.title: Start with the side chain
blocks.text: Amino acids share a backbone; the R group changes their behavior. Nonpolar side chains often pack inside water-soluble proteins. Charged or polar side chains can interact with water. The local environment and pH also matter.

blocks.title: Build the hierarchy
blocks.text: Primary structure is the amino-acid sequence linked by peptide bonds. Backbone hydrogen bonds stabilize alpha helices and beta sheets. Tertiary structure describes one chain’s overall fold; quaternary structure describes interactions between multiple chains.

blocks.title: Predict a perturbation
blocks.text: Ordinary heat or urea denaturation disrupts folding without cleaving peptide bonds. A reducing agent can break disulfide links between cysteines. Identify the bond affected before deciding which level of structure changes.

example.prompt: A two-subunit protein loses activity after heating, but each chain retains its sequence. Was its primary structure destroyed?
example.reasoning: No. Loss of activity can follow altered folding or subunit interactions. An intact sequence supports preserved primary structure; it does not establish a functional fold.

units.prediction: Predict what can happen to activity when the amino-acid sequence stays intact but the fold changes.

questions.stem: Which observation directly demonstrates a change in primary structure?
questions.explanation: Cleaving a peptide bond changes the covalent chain. The other changes can occur without altering the sequence.

questions.stem: Urea unfolds a protein without hydrolyzing it. Which feature is expected to persist?
questions.explanation: Unfolding disrupts higher-order structure; intact peptide bonds preserve the sequence.

questions.stem: A reducing agent separates two chains joined by cysteine residues. Which linkage was affected?
questions.explanation: A reducing agent breaks the covalent disulfide formed by two cysteine side chains. Hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, and hydrophobic interactions are noncovalent associations rather than this reducible linkage.

previousVersion.stem: A reducing agent separates two chains joined by cysteine residues. Which linkage was affected?
previousVersion.explanation: Oxidized cysteines can join through a disulfide. Reduction converts the linkage back to thiol groups.

questions.stem: A substitution introduces a charged residue into a buried nonpolar region. What is the best initial prediction?
options: The substitution leaves the primary structure unchanged
The new charge necessarily makes the native fold more stable
The substitution necessarily cleaves the nearby peptide backbone
questions.explanation: A changed side chain changes primary structure and can alter the energetic cost of burying that region. Stability may change, but its direction and any downstream dissociation require evidence; peptide cleavage is not implied.

previousVersion.stem: A substitution introduces a charged residue into a buried nonpolar region. What is the best initial prediction?
previousVersion.explanation: The side-chain environment becomes less favorable. A changed fold or stability is plausible; the more absolute outcomes are not established.

questions.stem: A protein retains its sequence but its two subunits separate. Which structural level is directly disrupted?
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure describes association between polypeptide subunits. Separation directly changes that association; the observation alone does not establish altered local helices or folding within each subunit.

previousVersion.stem: A protein retains its sequence but its two subunits separate. Which structural level is directly disrupted?
previousVersion.explanation: Quaternary structure describes interactions among separate polypeptide chains.

questions.stem: Hydrophobic side chains become exposed after unfolding in water. This primarily suggests a change in:
options: The order of residues in the polypeptide
The covalent identities of the exposed side chains
The number of residues in the polypeptide
questions.explanation: Exposing previously buried hydrophobic groups indicates altered folding and solvent accessibility. Unfolding alone does not establish sequence changes, chemical conversion of side chains, or peptide cleavage.

previousVersion.stem: Hydrophobic side chains become exposed after unfolding in water. This primarily suggests a change in:
previousVersion.explanation: Unfolding can alter which side chains contact water without changing the chain sequence.

units.title: Read an enzyme curve
units.subtitle: Separate substrate limitation, saturation, and competition.

blocks.title: Read the axes first
blocks.text: For a simple Michaelis–Menten enzyme, v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Vmax is the limiting rate at high substrate; Km is the substrate concentration at half that rate. This model does not describe every enzyme, including many cooperative enzymes.

blocks.title: Change one thing
blocks.text: A reversible competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km while preserving Vmax. At a fixed substrate concentration, the rate falls; sufficiently high substrate approaches the same plateau. Pure noncompetitive inhibition instead lowers Vmax with unchanged Km.

blocks.title: Keep rate and equilibrium separate
blocks.text: Enzymes lower the activation barrier. They do not change the reaction’s overall free-energy difference or equilibrium constant. A faster approach to equilibrium does not mean that equilibrium favors more product.

example.prompt: A curve has Vmax = 100 units/min and Km = 2 mM. What is v at [S] = 2 mM?
example.reasoning: v = 100 × 2 / (2 + 2) = 50 units/min. If competition doubles apparent Km to 4 mM, the rate at 2 mM is about 33.3; the limiting Vmax remains 100.

units.prediction: At the same substrate concentration, predict how adding a competitive inhibitor changes rate and the high-substrate plateau.

questions.stem: Where on a Michaelis–Menten curve is [S] equal to Km?
questions.explanation: Substituting [S] = Km gives v = Vmax/2.

questions.stem: With Vmax = 120 and Km = 3 mM, what is v at [S] = 3 mM?
questions.explanation: At Km, the rate is half of Vmax: 60.

questions.stem: An inhibitor shifts the curve right but leaves the plateau unchanged. Which model fits?
questions.explanation: In the simple models, competitive inhibition increases apparent Km while preserving Vmax. Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax; uncompetitive inhibition lowers both parameters. Adding enzyme raises Vmax rather than selectively shifting Km.

previousVersion.stem: An inhibitor shifts the curve right but leaves the plateau unchanged. Which model fits?
options: Irreversible loss of half the enzyme
previousVersion.explanation: More substrate is required for half-maximal rate, but Vmax is preserved.

questions.stem: Inhibitor X changes half-maximal substrate concentration from 2 to 8 mM; both curves plateau at 90. Which change is supported?
options: Vmax rises fourfold while Km is unchanged
Apparent Km falls fourfold while Vmax is unchanged
Apparent Km and Vmax both rise fourfold
questions.explanation: Half-maximal substrate concentration defines Km in this model: 8/2 = 4. The shared plateau indicates unchanged Vmax, so neither a Vmax change nor a fall in Km matches the data.

previousVersion.stem: Inhibitor X changes half-maximal substrate concentration from 2 to 8 mM; both curves plateau at 90. Which change is supported?
previousVersion.explanation: The half-maximal concentration measures apparent Km. The unchanged plateau identifies an unchanged Vmax.

questions.stem: Two simple enzyme curves share Vmax 200. Their half-maximal rates occur at 5 and 15 mM substrate. The second has:
questions.explanation: Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax. The ratio is 15/5 = 3; the explicitly shared Vmax rules out either plateau change.

previousVersion.stem: Two simple enzyme curves share Vmax 200. Their half-maximal rates occur at 5 and 15 mM substrate. The second has:
previousVersion.explanation: Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax; 15/5 = 3.

questions.stem: Pure noncompetitive inhibition reduces the plateau from 80 to 40 while half-maximal substrate concentration stays at 2 mM. What changed?
options: Km halved while Vmax stayed fixed
Km doubled while Vmax stayed fixed
questions.explanation: The plateau measures Vmax and falls by half. The substrate concentration at half of each curve’s own plateau remains 2 mM, indicating unchanged Km.

previousVersion.stem: Pure noncompetitive inhibition reduces the plateau from 80 to 40 while half-maximal substrate concentration stays at 2 mM. What changed?
previousVersion.explanation: A lower plateau indicates lower Vmax, with Km unchanged under the stated pure model.

units.title: Cross a membrane
units.subtitle: Use gradients and energy to explain movement.

blocks.title: Ask what can cross
blocks.text: Small nonpolar molecules can diffuse through a lipid bilayer. Ions usually need channels or transporters. A membrane is selectively permeable, so a concentration difference alone does not guarantee rapid movement.

blocks.title: Follow the driving force
blocks.text: Passive transport moves down a concentration gradient, or an electrochemical gradient for ions. Facilitated diffusion uses proteins without directly coupling transport to energy input. Primary active transport uses energy such as ATP; secondary active transport couples one gradient to another.

blocks.title: Track water separately
blocks.text: Osmosis is water movement across a selectively permeable membrane. Tonicity depends on effectively nonpenetrating solutes. In a simple ideal model, a cell placed in a solution with more nonpenetrating solute outside loses water.

example.prompt: Glucose uptake saturates and requires a transporter. Does saturation prove ATP is consumed?
example.reasoning: No. A limited number of transporters can saturate during facilitated diffusion. Determine the direction of transport and whether it couples to ATP or another gradient.

units.prediction: Predict whether using a membrane protein is enough to classify transport as active.

questions.stem: A transporter moves glucose down its concentration gradient without coupling to another process. This is:
questions.explanation: A protein can mediate passive transport. Down-gradient movement without energy coupling is facilitated diffusion.

questions.stem: A cell is placed in an ideal solution with more nonpenetrating solute outside. Initially, water tends to:
options: Show no net movement across the membrane
Leave until the cell becomes more dilute than its surroundings
questions.explanation: An initially higher concentration of nonpenetrating solute outside draws water out of a water-permeable cell. Water moves in both directions, but net movement is outward; losing water concentrates rather than dilutes the cell.

previousVersion.stem: A cell is placed in an ideal solution with more nonpenetrating solute outside. Initially, water tends to:
previousVersion.explanation: Water tends to leave toward the higher effective solute concentration.

questions.stem: An ion moves uphill while sodium moves downhill through the same cotransporter. What supplies the immediate driving force?
options: ATP hydrolysis at the cotransporter itself
The uphill ion’s concentration gradient alone
A chemical bond joining sodium to the transported ion
questions.explanation: Secondary active transport couples downhill sodium movement to uphill cargo movement. The sodium electrochemical gradient supplies the immediate energy; ATP may maintain that gradient elsewhere but is not hydrolyzed by this cotransport step.

previousVersion.stem: An ion moves uphill while sodium moves downhill through the same cotransporter. What supplies the immediate driving force?
options: A peptide bond in the cargo
previousVersion.explanation: Secondary active transport couples downhill movement to uphill movement. A pump may maintain the sodium gradient indirectly.

questions.stem: A channel opens, and an ion moves against its concentration gradient but down its electrical gradient. What else is needed to determine passive direction?
options: The concentration difference without considering voltage
The membrane voltage without considering concentration
The number of open channels without considering either gradient
questions.explanation: Passive ion movement depends on the net electrochemical gradient: the chemical and electrical contributions can oppose each other. Channel number affects conductance, not which competing gradient wins.

previousVersion.stem: A channel opens, and an ion moves against its concentration gradient but down its electrical gradient. What else is needed to determine passive direction?
previousVersion.explanation: Both concentration and voltage contribute to the net driving force for an ion.

questions.stem: A pump hydrolyzes ATP while moving an ion uphill. This is:
questions.explanation: Direct coupling of ATP hydrolysis to uphill transport is primary active transport. Secondary active transport instead uses another solute’s gradient; passive diffusion does not drive uphill electrochemical movement.

previousVersion.stem: A pump hydrolyzes ATP while moving an ion uphill. This is:
previousVersion.explanation: ATP directly supplies energy for primary active transport.

questions.stem: A solute gradient exists but the membrane is impermeable to that solute. Rapid equilibration by simple diffusion is:
options: Faster simply because the concentration gradient persists
Driven by the electrical gradient even without a permeation path
Expected to continue until solute concentrations are equal
Not established by the gradient alone
questions.explanation: A driving force cannot produce simple diffusion of a solute through a membrane that does not permit its passage. Permeability and a suitable driving force are both needed.

previousVersion.stem: A solute gradient exists but the membrane is impermeable to that solute. Rapid equilibration by simple diffusion is:
options: Not established by the gradient alone
previousVersion.explanation: Movement depends on both a driving force and a permeation pathway.

units.title: Balance a buffer
units.subtitle: Neutralize added acid first, then calculate pH.

blocks.title: Name both partners
blocks.text: A buffer pairs a weak acid HA with its conjugate base A−. Base consumes added H+ to form HA; acid consumes added OH− to form A− and water. A finite buffer can be exhausted.

blocks.title: Do stoichiometry first
blocks.text: For added strong acid, subtract its moles from A− and add those moles to HA. Only after neutralization use pH ≈ pKa + log10([A−]/[HA]). Moles give the same ratio when both species occupy the same volume.

blocks.title: Interpret the ratio
blocks.text: Equal acid and base give pH ≈ pKa. Ten times as much base gives pH ≈ pKa + 1. The approximation assumes a usable weak-acid buffer, both species remaining, and sufficiently ideal conditions. It fails after a component is exhausted.

example.prompt: A buffer has 0.20 mol A− and 0.20 mol HA, with pKa = 4.80. Add 0.10 mol HCl.
example.reasoning: Neutralization leaves 0.10 mol A− and 0.30 mol HA. pH ≈ 4.80 + log10(1/3) = 4.32. Using the original 1:1 ratio would miss the acid addition.

units.prediction: Predict which buffer component decreases when strong acid is added and whether pH rises or falls.

questions.stem: What should happen before applying the buffer equation after adding strong acid?
options: Use the original HA and A− amounts without adjustment
Update acid and base amounts by neutralization
Treat the added acid as if it remains entirely free in solution
Replace the weak acid pKa with the strong acid pKa
questions.explanation: Strong acid first consumes conjugate base and forms weak acid. Only after that stoichiometric update should the remaining buffer ratio be used; the original ratio and free strong-acid concentration do not describe the neutralized mixture.

previousVersion.stem: What should happen before applying the buffer equation after adding strong acid?
options: Update acid and base amounts by neutralization
previousVersion.explanation: The reaction changes the conjugate-pair ratio; use the remaining amounts.

questions.stem: A buffer contains equal HA and A−. Its pKa is 6.2. Approximate pH is:
questions.explanation: log10(1) = 0, so pH equals pKa.

questions.stem: Add 0.02 mol H+ to 0.10 mol A− and 0.10 mol HA. What remains?
questions.explanation: A− consumes H+ and becomes HA: subtract from base and add to acid.

questions.stem: A buffer with pKa 5.0 contains 0.30 mol A− and 0.10 mol HA. Add 0.10 mol strong acid. Approximate final pH is:
questions.explanation: Both species end at 0.20 mol. The ratio is one, so pH is approximately 5.0.

questions.stem: A buffer starts with 0.15 mol HA and 0.15 mol A−. Add 0.05 mol OH−. Remaining HA and A− are:
questions.explanation: OH− consumes HA and forms A−; subtract from acid and add to base.

questions.stem: After neutralization, A−/HA = 10 and pKa = 4.2. Approximate pH is:
questions.explanation: The ratio is 10, so log10(10) is 1. Add that to pKa: 4.2 + 1 = 5.2. More conjugate base than acid raises pH above pKa.

units.title: Follow current through a circuit
units.subtitle: Change a branch and see what happens to resistance and current.

blocks.title: Define the quantities
blocks.text: Voltage is energy per charge; current is charge per time. For an ideal ohmic resistor, V = IR. Power dissipated is P = VI = I²R. Keep volts, amperes, ohms, and watts distinct.

blocks.title: Compare the connections
blocks.text: Series resistors carry the same current and their resistances add. Parallel branches share the same voltage; reciprocal resistances add. The equivalent resistance of two positive parallel resistors is less than either branch resistance.

blocks.title: State the source assumption
blocks.text: With an ideal battery holding voltage constant, adding a parallel branch reduces equivalent resistance and raises total current. Current in an unchanged branch stays the same. A real source with internal resistance can behave differently.

example.prompt: A 12 V ideal battery feeds 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel. Find total current.
example.reasoning: 1/Req = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so Req = 2 Ω. Total current = 12/2 = 6 A. Branch currents are 2 A and 4 A, which sum to 6 A.

units.prediction: With battery voltage fixed, predict how total current changes when you switch two resistors from series to parallel.

questions.stem: Two resistors connected in parallel share the same:
questions.explanation: Each branch connects across the same two nodes, so it has the same potential difference.

questions.stem: A 12 V source drives 4 Ω and 8 Ω in series. The current is:
questions.explanation: Series resistance is 12 Ω; I = 12 V / 12 Ω = 1 A.

questions.stem: An ideal battery gains a parallel branch while voltage stays fixed. Total current:
questions.explanation: The added conducting path lowers equivalent resistance; fixed V and smaller R imply higher total I.

questions.stem: Two 8 Ω resistors in parallel connect to 12 V. Total power is:
questions.explanation: Req = 4 Ω, so P = V²/R = 144/4 = 36 W.

questions.stem: Two 4 Ω resistors in series connect to 16 V. Total current is:
questions.explanation: Series resistance is 8 Ω, so I = 16/8 = 2 A.

questions.stem: A fixed-voltage ideal circuit gains a parallel branch. Current in an unchanged original branch:
questions.explanation: The original branch retains the same voltage and resistance, so its current is unchanged.

units.title: Separate speed from destination
units.subtitle: Distinguish activation barriers, equilibrium, and reaction direction.

blocks.title: A fast reaction is not necessarily favored
blocks.text: Kinetics describes rate. Thermodynamics describes energetic favorability and equilibrium. A reaction can be favorable yet slow because its activation barrier is high.

blocks.title: Compare Q with K
blocks.text: Q uses the current activities, approximated by suitable concentration or pressure ratios. At fixed temperature, Q < K favors net forward reaction; Q > K favors net reverse reaction. At equilibrium Q = K, with equal forward and reverse rates.

blocks.title: Understand a catalyst
blocks.text: A catalyst supplies a path with a lower activation barrier for both directions. It speeds approach to equilibrium without changing K or the standard reaction free-energy difference. Changing temperature can change K.

example.prompt: Two sealed mixtures have identical starting composition and temperature. One receives a catalyst. Must its final equilibrium contain more product?
example.reasoning: No. It can approach equilibrium faster, but the catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant. Compare compositions after equilibration, not only at an early observation time.

units.prediction: Predict whether a catalyst changes the time to equilibrium, the equilibrium composition, or both.

questions.stem: At fixed temperature, a catalyst changes which quantity directly?
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides a lower-barrier pathway for forward and reverse reactions. At fixed temperature it changes how quickly equilibrium is approached, not the thermodynamic equilibrium constant or standard reaction free energy.

previousVersion.stem: At fixed temperature, a catalyst changes which quantity directly?
previousVersion.explanation: A catalyst changes the reaction path and activation barrier, not the equilibrium thermodynamics.

questions.stem: For a reaction with Q < K, the net reaction initially proceeds:
options: With equal forward and reverse rates
In a direction determined by the catalyst used
questions.explanation: Q below K means the mixture has less product relative to reactant than at equilibrium, so net forward reaction is favored. Equal rates occur at Q = K; a catalyst does not select a different equilibrium direction.

previousVersion.stem: For a reaction with Q < K, the net reaction initially proceeds:
previousVersion.explanation: Forward reaction raises Q toward K under the stated conditions.

questions.stem: At dynamic equilibrium, which statement is correct?
options: Forward and reverse rates are equal
questions.explanation: Both directions continue at equal rates; concentrations need not equal one another.

questions.stem: A catalyzed vessel has more product after one minute but the same product amount after a day as an uncatalyzed vessel. This supports:
options: A faster approach to the same equilibrium
questions.explanation: The early difference indicates kinetics; the shared equilibrated composition is consistent with unchanged K.

questions.stem: A mixture has Q greater than K at fixed temperature. Net reaction initially favors:
options: An equilibrium composition with equal concentrations
A direction determined by which catalyst is present
questions.explanation: When Q exceeds K, net reverse reaction lowers the product-to-reactant ratio toward its equilibrium value. Equilibrium does not require equal concentrations, and a catalyst does not change K.

previousVersion.stem: A mixture has Q greater than K at fixed temperature. Net reaction initially favors:
previousVersion.explanation: Net reverse reaction lowers Q toward K.

questions.stem: Two catalysts give different rates for the same reaction at the same temperature. Equilibrium constants should:
options: Be larger for the catalyst giving the faster rate
Be smaller for the catalyst giving the faster rate
Vary with catalyst concentration at fixed temperature
questions.explanation: For the same reaction at a fixed temperature, K is set by thermodynamics. Different catalytic pathways or catalyst amounts change rates without changing that equilibrium constant.

previousVersion.stem: Two catalysts give different rates for the same reaction at the same temperature. Equilibrium constants should:
options: Differ in direct proportion to rates
previousVersion.explanation: Catalysts change kinetic paths, not the equilibrium constant for the reaction.

units.title: Read a behavioral consequence
units.subtitle: Track what is added or removed and whether behavior increases.

blocks.title: Observe the change in behavior
blocks.text: Operant conditioning links behavior to consequences. Reinforcement increases future behavior; punishment decreases it. Positive means a stimulus is added, while negative means one is removed. Those words do not mean good and bad.

blocks.title: Classify in two steps
blocks.text: First determine whether behavior increased or decreased. Then determine whether the consequence added or removed a stimulus. Removing an unpleasant stimulus can reinforce behavior; removing a valued stimulus can punish it.

blocks.title: Read the schedule
blocks.text: Ratio schedules depend on response count; interval schedules depend on elapsed time before an eligible response. Fixed schedules are predictable; variable schedules vary. Unpredictable response counts characterize variable-ratio reinforcement.

example.prompt: A car’s beeping stops when the driver buckles up, and buckling becomes more frequent.
example.reasoning: The behavior increases, so this is reinforcement. The consequence removes the beep, so it is negative reinforcement. The beep being unpleasant does not make the consequence punishment.

units.prediction: Predict how you would distinguish negative reinforcement from punishment using observed behavior.

questions.stem: An unpleasant sound stops after a response, and the response becomes more frequent. This is:
questions.explanation: Removal plus increased behavior defines negative reinforcement.

questions.stem: A student loses game access after interrupting, and interrupting decreases. This is:
questions.explanation: A valued stimulus is removed and the behavior decreases.

questions.stem: Rewards arrive after an unpredictable number of responses. Which schedule is this?
questions.explanation: Response count identifies ratio; unpredictability identifies variable.

questions.stem: A coach adds extra laps after lateness, and lateness decreases. Which classification fits the observed effect?
questions.explanation: A consequence is added and behavior decreases: positive punishment.

questions.stem: A reward arrives after every tenth response. The schedule is:
questions.explanation: A predictable number of responses defines a fixed-ratio schedule.

questions.stem: A child receives praise after helping, and helping increases. This is:
questions.explanation: A stimulus is added and the behavior increases.

units.title: Build and retrieve a memory
units.subtitle: Separate encoding, storage, and access.

blocks.title: Follow the process
blocks.text: Encoding converts an experience into a usable representation. Storage maintains information over time; retrieval brings it into use. Failure to recall can reflect a problem at any of these stages.

blocks.title: Identify the system
blocks.text: Explicit memory includes episodic experiences and semantic facts. Implicit memory includes learned skills and some conditioning effects. A person can improve at a skill without consciously remembering the training episodes.

blocks.title: Use the retrieval context
blocks.text: A context can cue access to a stored memory. Better recall in a matching environment is compatible with context-dependent retrieval; it does not show that the person learned nothing elsewhere. Recognition and free recall place different demands on retrieval.

example.prompt: A participant improves at mirror tracing across days but cannot remember attending the sessions.
example.reasoning: Skill improvement supports preserved procedural learning. Poor conscious recollection indicates a difficulty with explicit memory. The dissociation argues against treating all memory as one process.

units.prediction: Predict whether inability to recall a training session necessarily prevents improvement on a practiced motor skill.

questions.stem: Remembering your first day of college is primarily an example of:
questions.explanation: An autobiographical event is episodic memory. Semantic memory stores general knowledge, procedural memory supports practiced skills, and working memory temporarily holds information for current use.

previousVersion.stem: Remembering your first day of college is primarily an example of:
previousVersion.explanation: A personally experienced event is episodic memory.

questions.stem: Knowing the meaning of a word is primarily:
questions.explanation: Word meaning is general factual knowledge, characteristic of semantic memory. Remembering a specific occasion of learning it would be episodic; a practiced motor routine or fleeting sensory trace is a different memory type.

previousVersion.stem: Knowing the meaning of a word is primarily:
previousVersion.explanation: Semantic memory supports facts and meanings without requiring recollection of a particular learning episode.

questions.stem: A learned skill improves without conscious memory of practice. This most directly distinguishes:
questions.explanation: Learning expressed through performance without conscious recollection supports the implicit–explicit distinction. Episodic and semantic memory are both explicit categories; recognition versus recall concerns retrieval tasks.

previousVersion.stem: A learned skill improves without conscious memory of practice. This most directly distinguishes:
previousVersion.explanation: Performance can express implicit learning even when explicit recollection is impaired.

questions.stem: A list learned in a particular room is recalled better in that room than elsewhere. The room most plausibly acts as:
options: Evidence of a larger working-memory capacity
Evidence that the room lengthens sensory storage
Evidence that changing rooms erases the stored list
questions.explanation: The room can supply contextual retrieval cues. Better access in the original setting does not establish changed capacity, longer sensory storage, or destruction of the memory elsewhere.

previousVersion.stem: A list learned in a particular room is recalled better in that room than elsewhere. The room most plausibly acts as:
previousVersion.explanation: Matching context can support access to stored information.

questions.stem: A pianist performs a practiced scale without recalling learning each movement. The performance draws heavily on:
options: Episodic memory for the practice sessions
Echoic storage of the last sound heard
questions.explanation: Executing a well-practiced motor sequence relies heavily on procedural memory. It does not require autobiographical recollection, a verbal definition, or a brief auditory sensory trace.

previousVersion.stem: A pianist performs a practiced scale without recalling learning each movement. The performance draws heavily on:
previousVersion.explanation: Learned motor skills are an example of implicit procedural memory.

questions.stem: A learner recognizes an answer among options but cannot freely recall it. The two tasks differ in:
options: Whether the material was encoded in the first place
Whether the stored information is autobiographical
Whether the learning involved a motor skill
questions.explanation: Recognition supplies candidate answers that act as retrieval cues. A recognition–recall difference does not by itself identify encoding success, memory content, or motor learning.

previousVersion.stem: A learner recognizes an answer among options but cannot freely recall it. The two tasks differ in:
previousVersion.explanation: Recognition supplies cues that free recall does not.

units.title: Decide what a study can claim
units.subtitle: Use learning and memory experiments to practice research reasoning.

blocks.title: Separate sampling from assignment
blocks.text: Random sampling concerns who enters a study and can support generalization. Random assignment concerns which condition participants receive and helps balance confounders in expectation. Neither guarantees a perfectly representative sample or perfectly balanced groups.

blocks.title: Match the claim to the design
blocks.text: A correlation identifies an association. Reverse causation and common causes can remain possible. Manipulation with random assignment and suitable controls can strengthen causal inference, subject to implementation and measurement limitations.

blocks.title: Inspect the comparison
blocks.text: An active control can match time, attention, or expectations. Define the outcome operationally: for a memory intervention, count words recalled after a fixed delay. Distinguish the manipulated factor from the measured response.

example.prompt: Students choose either a memory workshop or no workshop. Workshop students later recall more words. Does the difference isolate the workshop’s causal effect?
example.reasoning: No. Self-selection leaves alternatives such as prior motivation. Random assignment and a comparison activity matched for time and attention would address important alternatives, though design limitations still need evaluation.

units.prediction: Predict why letting participants choose a condition can complicate a causal claim.

questions.stem: Random assignment primarily helps with which goal?
options: Making the sample representative of its target population
Balancing potential confounders across conditions in expectation
Keeping the outcome instrument calibrated across sessions
Preventing participants from knowing their treatment
questions.explanation: Random assignment balances potential confounders between conditions in expectation. Representative sampling, instrument calibration, and blinding address separate problems and do not follow automatically from randomization.

previousVersion.stem: Random assignment primarily helps with which goal?
options: Balancing potential confounders across conditions in expectation
previousVersion.explanation: Assignment addresses group comparability; sampling addresses representation.

questions.stem: In a study manipulating sleep duration and measuring words recalled, the dependent variable is:
questions.explanation: The measured outcome is recall; assigned sleep is the independent variable.

questions.stem: A survey finds study time and grades are correlated. Which statement is justified by this alone?
options: Increasing study time would necessarily increase grades
Higher grades are what caused students to study longer
The association would persist after controlling prior preparation
questions.explanation: Correlation establishes an observed association. Either causal direction or a third variable could explain it, and the association after adjustment has not been reported.

previousVersion.stem: A survey finds study time and grades are correlated. Which statement is justified by this alone?
options: Study time causes all grade differences
previousVersion.explanation: Correlation alone leaves causal direction and common causes unresolved.

questions.stem: A memory course is compared with no contact. Which addition best addresses the effect of instructor attention?
options: An active comparison with similar instructor contact
questions.explanation: Matched contact helps distinguish attention effects from the course’s specific content.

questions.stem: Participants are randomly sampled but choose their treatment. Which concern remains for comparing treatment effects?
options: That random sampling also randomized treatment choice
That a representative sample removes confounding between treatments
That equal group sizes would eliminate selection differences
questions.explanation: Random sampling supports population representation but does not randomly assign treatment. People choosing different treatments may differ in outcome-relevant ways, even with equal group sizes.

previousVersion.stem: Participants are randomly sampled but choose their treatment. Which concern remains for comparing treatment effects?
options: No possibility of generalization at all
previousVersion.explanation: Random sampling and random assignment serve different goals; condition choice permits self-selection.

questions.stem: A study manipulates study schedule while measuring recall after one week. Study schedule is the:
questions.explanation: The researcher deliberately varies study schedule, making it the independent variable. Recall is the measured dependent variable; a confound would vary with the manipulation and offer an alternative explanation.

previousVersion.stem: A study manipulates study schedule while measuring recall after one week. Study schedule is the:
previousVersion.explanation: The manipulated factor is the independent variable; delayed recall is the outcome.

units.title: Find the author’s claim
units.subtitle: Track the argument before judging the topic.

blocks.title: Give each paragraph a job
blocks.text: Identify whether a paragraph introduces a question, gives evidence, presents an objection, or qualifies a claim. A repeated subject tells you the topic; the author’s position tells you the thesis.

blocks.title: Preserve qualifications
blocks.text: Words such as sometimes, mainly, and unless define scope. An answer can echo a passage’s vocabulary while overstating its claim. Judge the whole answer against the whole passage.

blocks.title: Use evidence from the text
blocks.text: For comprehension, ground the answer in what the passage says or clearly implies. Outside facts can distract from the author’s actual argument. These short examples introduce the skill; full passages provide a more demanding application.

example.prompt: “Public gardens are often praised for beauty. Yet their greater value may be social: shared maintenance gives neighbors a reason to cooperate. Beauty matters, but it is not their only benefit.” What is the main claim?
example.reasoning: Gardens can promote social cooperation as well as provide beauty. The author qualifies the aesthetic account, without rejecting beauty or claiming that every garden creates community.

units.prediction: Predict why “gardens have no aesthetic value” misrepresents the excerpt.

questions.stem: “Libraries lend books, but their public meeting spaces also sustain civic life.” Which summary preserves the claim?
options: Libraries’ civic value comes chiefly from lending books
Libraries’ meeting spaces matter more than their lending services
Libraries serve lending and civic roles
Libraries sustain civic life only when they provide meeting spaces
questions.explanation: The statement gives libraries both lending and civic functions. It does not rank one above the other, reduce civic value to lending, or make meeting spaces necessary for every civic contribution.

previousVersion.stem: “Libraries lend books, but their public meeting spaces also sustain civic life.” Which summary preserves the claim?
options: Libraries serve lending and civic roles
previousVersion.explanation: The sentence adds a civic role while retaining lending.

questions.stem: “Some traditions deserve revision, though age alone is no reason to reject them.” The author supports:
options: Older traditions deserve more protection than newer ones
Traditions should be revised once their origins are forgotten
A tradition should be retained unless it is demonstrably harmful
questions.explanation: The author permits revision while rejecting age alone as a reason for it. No preference for older traditions, rule about forgotten origins, or specific burden of proof is supplied.

previousVersion.stem: “Some traditions deserve revision, though age alone is no reason to reject them.” The author supports:
previousVersion.explanation: The qualification rejects age as a sufficient reason, without protecting all traditions.

questions.stem: A paragraph states a critic’s position and then identifies its limits. Its primary role is to:
options: Adopt the critic’s position as the final conclusion
Explain the historical origin of the critic’s position
Use the critic’s position as an example supporting an earlier claim
questions.explanation: Introducing an objection and identifying its limits presents and qualifies that objection. The described structure does not establish endorsement, historical explanation, or agreement with an earlier claim.

previousVersion.stem: A paragraph states a critic’s position and then identifies its limits. Its primary role is to:
options: Prove the critic authored the passage
previousVersion.explanation: Rhetorical function concerns what the paragraph does in the argument.

questions.stem: “Digital archives widen access, although finding a record still requires careful cataloging.” Best summary?
options: Digital archives improve access by reducing the need for cataloging
Careful cataloging is what makes an archive digital
Access improves, with discovery still depending on organization
Digitization improves access only when every record is fully cataloged
questions.explanation: The author grants wider access while retaining a qualification about discovery. The statement does not make cataloging unnecessary, define digitization by cataloging, or require a completely finished catalog before any benefit.

previousVersion.stem: “Digital archives widen access, although finding a record still requires careful cataloging.” Best summary?
options: Digital records are always easy to find
Access improves, with discovery still depending on organization
previousVersion.explanation: Both the benefit and the qualification belong in the summary.

questions.stem: “Public debates can inform citizens, though slogans sometimes crowd out detail.” Best summary?
options: Debates inform citizens chiefly through memorable slogans
Debates are informative only when slogans are absent
Debates can inform despite limits in depth
The chief purpose of public debate is to communicate detail
questions.explanation: The author allows an informational benefit while acknowledging a limitation. The statement neither credits slogans with that benefit nor says slogans must be absent for a debate to inform.

previousVersion.stem: “Public debates can inform citizens, though slogans sometimes crowd out detail.” Best summary?
options: Debates can inform despite limits in depth
previousVersion.explanation: The summary preserves both the potential benefit and the qualification.

questions.stem: A paragraph offers a concrete case after a broad claim. Its likely role is to:
options: Establish that the claim has no exceptions
Replace the broad claim with a narrower definition
Explain why the author rejects the broad claim
questions.explanation: A concrete case can illustrate a general claim. One example does not establish universality, redefine the claim, or show rejection without further context.

previousVersion.stem: A paragraph offers a concrete case after a broad claim. Its likely role is to:
previousVersion.explanation: A relevant example can make the preceding general claim concrete.

units.title: Test an argument from within
units.subtitle: Identify support, assumptions, and warranted inferences.

blocks.title: Separate claim from support
blocks.text: A claim is what the author wants you to accept. Evidence supplies a reason. An assumption bridges the evidence and claim, sometimes without being stated explicitly.

blocks.title: Prefer warranted inference
blocks.text: Choose what the passage supports with the fewest additional assumptions. An inference can go beyond an exact quotation while remaining constrained by the argument. A possible explanation is not automatically a necessary one.

blocks.title: Evaluate the link
blocks.text: To weaken an argument, look for a fact that undermines the connection between evidence and conclusion. A new fact about the topic may be irrelevant to that connection. To strengthen it, address the same inferential gap.

example.prompt: “Attendance rose after the museum extended its hours, so the longer hours caused the increase.” Which new fact most weakens the causal inference?
example.reasoning: A major free exhibition opened at the same time. It offers an alternative explanation for the attendance increase; it does not prove that longer hours had no effect.

units.prediction: Predict why identifying an alternative explanation weakens a causal inference without necessarily disproving it.

questions.stem: An author concludes a new policy caused an improvement because the improvement followed it. Which issue is most relevant?
options: Whether another change occurred at the same time
Whether the policy received favorable coverage
Whether the improvement was large enough to attract attention
Whether the author personally supported the policy
questions.explanation: Another simultaneous change offers an alternative cause. Popularity, visibility, and the author’s preference do not resolve the gap between temporal sequence and causal attribution.

previousVersion.stem: An author concludes a new policy caused an improvement because the improvement followed it. Which issue is most relevant?
options: Whether another change occurred at the same time
Whether the policy has a short name
previousVersion.explanation: A simultaneous change could explain the improvement and challenge the causal link.

questions.stem: “All exhibits in this room are replicas. This vase is in this room.” Which inference follows?
options: Every replica in the museum is a vase
This vase is a replica of another exhibit in the same room
Every vase in the museum is in this room
questions.explanation: The universal claim applies to this vase because it is in the stated room. It does not identify the original’s location, characterize every replica, or place every vase in that room.

previousVersion.stem: “All exhibits in this room are replicas. This vase is in this room.” Which inference follows?
previousVersion.explanation: The stated rule applies to this vase, not to all vases or the entire museum.

questions.stem: A critic says short reviews are always superficial. A carefully reasoned short review would function as:
options: An example confirming the critic’s generalization
A reason to redefine superficiality as brevity
Evidence that long reviews are usually superficial
questions.explanation: One substantive short review is enough to refute the universal claim that short reviews are always superficial. It does not establish a general claim about long reviews or require changing the meaning of superficiality.

previousVersion.stem: A critic says short reviews are always superficial. A carefully reasoned short review would function as:
previousVersion.explanation: One relevant counterexample can challenge an unqualified universal claim.

questions.stem: A writer argues volunteers are reliable because those interviewed attended every meeting. Which assumption needs scrutiny?
options: Interviewees adequately represent the volunteers under discussion
Attending meetings necessarily makes interview answers accurate
The organization’s meetings were held at regular intervals
The interviews occurred before the final meeting
questions.explanation: The argument generalizes from those interviewed to the broader volunteer group. Their representativeness is the relevant assumption; scheduling and interview timing do not establish it.

previousVersion.stem: A writer argues volunteers are reliable because those interviewed attended every meeting. Which assumption needs scrutiny?
options: Interviewees adequately represent the volunteers under discussion
previousVersion.explanation: The general conclusion depends on how well the evidence supports the broader group.

questions.stem: An author says a policy is popular because all five interviewed supporters favor it. The main gap is:
options: Whether the supporters gave detailed reasons for their views
Whether the same five supporters were interviewed twice
Whether the policy had already been implemented
Whether the sample supports the population claim
questions.explanation: A sample consisting only of supporters cannot establish popularity in the broader population. More detail or repeat interviews with the same selected people does not repair that sampling gap.

previousVersion.stem: An author says a policy is popular because all five interviewed supporters favor it. The main gap is:
options: Whether the sample supports the population claim
previousVersion.explanation: Interviewing only supporters does not establish broad popularity.

questions.stem: “Every member submitted a report; Lina is a member.” Which conclusion is warranted?
options: Everyone who submitted a report is a member
Lina’s report was submitted before the other members’ reports
questions.explanation: Membership places Lina within the group required by the premise to have submitted. The statement does not say that only members submitted, specify the number of reports, or establish their order.

previousVersion.stem: “Every member submitted a report; Lina is a member.” Which conclusion is warranted?
previousVersion.explanation: The stated universal rule applies to Lina without adding further claims.

units.title: Carry a principle into a new case
units.subtitle: Apply the author’s reasoning without changing its conditions.

blocks.title: Extract a conditional principle
blocks.text: Turn the author’s reasoning into an if–then relationship when possible. Retain the conditions that made the original claim plausible. A slogan that drops those conditions can produce the wrong application.

blocks.title: Match structure over surface
blocks.text: A strong analogy preserves the relevant relationships, even when the setting changes. A weak analogy may repeat the same nouns while changing the cause, goal, or constraint.

blocks.title: Test new information
blocks.text: Ask whether a new case meets the principle’s conditions. Evidence that violates a key condition can limit an application. New evidence may revise the argument without implying that every claim in the passage is false.

example.prompt: A writer argues that local decision-making works best when residents possess relevant knowledge and bear the consequences. Would that principle automatically endorse every local vote?
example.reasoning: No. The application depends on the specified knowledge and consequences. A local vote on a problem whose harms fall mainly on distant communities may fail the second condition.

units.prediction: Predict which matters more for an analogy: shared vocabulary or shared relationships.

questions.stem: A passage favors transparency when outsiders cannot otherwise assess decisions. Which new case best fits?
options: Publishing reasons for an opaque grant decision
Publishing a grant outcome while withholding its reasons
Explaining a grant’s purpose without explaining its selection
Asking grant applicants to trust the committee’s expertise
questions.explanation: Publishing reasons lets outsiders assess an otherwise opaque decision. Outcomes, general purposes, and assurances of expertise do not expose the decision’s reasoning.

previousVersion.stem: A passage favors transparency when outsiders cannot otherwise assess decisions. Which new case best fits?
options: Publishing reasons for an opaque grant decision
previousVersion.explanation: The new case addresses the same information gap through transparency.

questions.stem: An author supports experimentation when errors are reversible. Which case most clearly fails that stated condition?
questions.explanation: Irreversible demolition violates the reversibility condition.

questions.stem: A strong analogy primarily preserves:
options: Matching the original example’s subject matter
Using the same favorable outcome as the original example
Keeping the original actors’ social roles
questions.explanation: A useful analogy carries the relationships and constraints relevant to the argument. Shared topic, outcome, or social roles alone can leave the central reasoning unmatched.

previousVersion.stem: A strong analogy primarily preserves:
previousVersion.explanation: Analogical reasoning depends on structural similarity relevant to the claim.

questions.stem: A writer endorses competition only when participants can enter on equal terms. Which policy best matches?
options: Giving incumbents extra entries to reward experience
Using identical scoring rules while restricting entry to members
Awarding prizes equally while leaving entry restrictions in place
questions.explanation: The principle concerns equal entry conditions. Fair-looking scoring or prizes do not repair arbitrary barriers that prevent some participants from entering.

previousVersion.stem: A writer endorses competition only when participants can enter on equal terms. Which policy best matches?
previousVersion.explanation: Reducing arbitrary barriers supports the stated equal-entry condition.

questions.stem: A writer favors preserving old buildings when they can safely serve a community need. Which case best fits?
options: A structurally unsafe historic hall kept open for occasional tours
A safe historic school converted into a library
A safe historic warehouse left unused despite conversion proposals
An old library preserved despite unresolved structural hazards
questions.explanation: The converted school satisfies both safety and community use. Age alone, safety without use, or use despite unresolved hazards each omits one of the principle’s conditions.

previousVersion.stem: A writer favors preserving old buildings when they can safely serve a community need. Which case best fits?
options: A safe historic school converted into a library
An unsafe building with no possible use
previousVersion.explanation: The case meets both the safety and community-use conditions.

questions.stem: A principle values decentralization only when decisions mainly affect local residents. Which new case challenges its application?
options: Local choices impose major harms downstream on outsiders
A village selects its meeting time
questions.explanation: The external harms violate the principle’s condition about who bears the consequences.

units.title: Account for glycolysis
units.subtitle: Follow carbon and distinguish investment from payoff.

blocks.title: Keep a ledger
blocks.text: One glucose becomes two three-carbon pyruvates in the cytosol. Two ATP are invested and four are formed, giving a net two ATP. Two NAD+ accept electrons to become two NADH.

blocks.title: Separate ATP mechanisms
blocks.text: Substrate-level phosphorylation transfers phosphate from a metabolic intermediate to ADP. It does not require the respiratory chain. Glycolysis can continue without oxygen if the cell regenerates NAD+.

blocks.title: Connect a constraint
blocks.text: During lactate fermentation, pyruvate accepts electrons from NADH. This restores NAD+ for glycolysis; the fermentation step itself adds no extra ATP. Blocking NAD+ regeneration eventually limits the oxidation step in glycolysis.

example.prompt: A cell converts one glucose to two lactates. Does fermentation add ATP beyond glycolysis?
example.reasoning: No. The net ATP comes from glycolysis. Reducing pyruvate to lactate restores NAD+, allowing glycolysis to continue.

units.prediction: A cell converts one glucose to two lactates. Does fermentation add ATP beyond glycolysis? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Net ATP from glycolysis per glucose is:
questions.explanation: Four ATP are formed after two are invested, leaving two net.

questions.stem: Where does glycolysis occur in a eukaryotic cell?
questions.explanation: Glycolytic enzymes operate in the cytosol.

questions.stem: Reducing pyruvate to lactate primarily regenerates:
questions.explanation: Lactate formation consumes NADH and pyruvate while regenerating NAD+, which supports the oxidation step of glycolysis. The lactate-forming step itself does not generate ATP.

previousVersion.stem: Reducing pyruvate to lactate primarily regenerates:
previousVersion.explanation: NADH donates electrons and becomes NAD+, which glycolysis requires.

questions.stem: Three glucose molecules complete glycolysis. What is the net ATP yield?
questions.explanation: Each glucose yields two net ATP, so three yield six.

questions.stem: A cell cannot regenerate NAD+. Which glycolytic step directly requires that cofactor?
options: The initial phosphorylation of glucose by ATP
The conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate
The cleavage of fructose bisphosphate into three-carbon sugars
questions.explanation: The glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate oxidation directly requires NAD+. The other named reactions do not directly use NAD+, although disruption of one step can eventually limit overall pathway flux.

previousVersion.stem: A cell has abundant glucose but cannot regenerate NAD+. Which process becomes limited?
previousVersion.explanation: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate oxidation requires NAD+; depletion limits continued flux.

questions.stem: A tracer follows six glucose carbons through glycolysis alone. The principal carbon products are:
questions.explanation: Glycolysis splits and rearranges the six-carbon sugar into two pyruvates without releasing CO2.

units.title: Link electrons to ATP
units.subtitle: Predict how transport, gradients, and ATP synthesis depend on one another.

blocks.title: Deliver reducing equivalents
blocks.text: Pyruvate oxidation produces acetyl-CoA, CO2, and NADH. The citric acid cycle oxidizes acetyl groups, producing CO2, NADH, FADH2, and a small amount of GTP or ATP.

blocks.title: Build the gradient
blocks.text: Respiratory-chain electron transfers drive proton pumping from matrix to intermembrane space. Oxygen accepts electrons at the end and is reduced to water. ATP synthase uses proton flow back toward the matrix.

blocks.title: Distinguish two disruptions
blocks.text: A respiratory-chain inhibitor can reduce electron transport and oxygen consumption. An uncoupler dissipates the proton gradient: electron transport may accelerate while ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation falls. Substrate supply and oxygen availability still constrain the response.

example.prompt: An uncoupler lowers ATP production while oxygen consumption rises. Is that internally consistent?
example.reasoning: Yes. Electron transport can proceed faster as the gradient dissipates, but the gradient is no longer efficiently captured to synthesize ATP.

units.prediction: An uncoupler lowers ATP production while oxygen consumption rises. Is that internally consistent? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: The final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration is:
questions.explanation: Oxygen receives electrons at the terminal complex and is reduced to water.

questions.stem: ATP synthase is directly driven by:
options: Electron transfer directly from NADH to ATP
Hydrolysis of a high-energy bond in glucose
Diffusion of oxygen through the membrane
questions.explanation: ATP synthase couples proton movement down an electrochemical gradient to ATP synthesis. The respiratory chain builds the gradient; electrons do not transfer directly into ATP, and glucose or oxygen diffusion does not directly power the synthase.

previousVersion.stem: ATP synthase is directly driven by:
previousVersion.explanation: Proton flow down its gradient supplies energy for ATP synthesis.

questions.stem: A protonophore uncoupler most directly dissipates:
options: The NADH pool by binding NADH irreversibly
The oxygen concentration by blocking its entry
The ATP pool by directly hydrolyzing ATP
questions.explanation: A protonophore uncoupler permits proton movement across the inner membrane, dissipating the gradient that drives ATP synthesis. It does not act by directly hydrolyzing ATP or preventing oxygen entry.

previousVersion.stem: An uncoupler most directly dissipates:
previousVersion.explanation: An uncoupler permits proton return without productive ATP synthesis.

questions.stem: A membrane becomes permeable to protons. ATP falls despite an active respiratory chain. The most direct explanation is:
options: A higher ATP yield for each oxygen molecule consumed
An increase in the membrane’s ability to retain protons
questions.explanation: A proton leak dissipates the coupling gradient, so respiration can continue with less ATP production. The observation does not require glycolytic inhibition and predicts reduced, rather than increased, coupling efficiency.

previousVersion.stem: A membrane becomes permeable to protons. ATP falls despite an active respiratory chain. The most direct explanation is:
previousVersion.explanation: A leaky membrane cannot maintain the proton gradient needed for efficient coupling.

questions.stem: A block at the terminal electron-transfer complex prevents transfer to oxygen. Oxygen consumption should initially:
options: Remain at its previous rate despite the blocked transfer
Increase enough to compensate for reduced ATP production
questions.explanation: Blocking electron transfer to oxygen reduces its consumption by the respiratory chain. Accumulating upstream electrons cannot bypass the stated terminal block simply because ATP demand rises.

previousVersion.stem: A block at the terminal electron-transfer complex prevents transfer to oxygen. Oxygen consumption should initially:
previousVersion.explanation: Blocking electron transfer to oxygen limits respiratory oxygen consumption.

questions.stem: A cell increases citric-cycle flux. Which output directly supplies electrons to the respiratory chain?
questions.explanation: NADH and FADH2 carry reducing equivalents from the cycle to respiratory electron transfer. Nucleoside triphosphates store transferable energy, while CO2 and cycle intermediates are not the carriers asked for.

previousVersion.stem: A cell increases citric-cycle flux. Which output directly supplies electrons to the respiratory chain?
previousVersion.explanation: Reduced electron carriers convey electrons to the chain.

units.title: Choose a fuel pathway
units.subtitle: Connect energy state to pathway regulation.

blocks.title: Read feedback
blocks.text: A pathway responds to energy demand and substrate availability. High ATP can inhibit key catabolic enzymes; ADP or AMP can signal demand. The effect depends on the particular enzyme and tissue.

blocks.title: Coordinate the fed state
blocks.text: Insulin generally promotes glucose use and storage after feeding. Glycogen synthesis stores glucose units; fatty-acid synthesis stores energy in another form. A pathway diagram should distinguish storage from immediate oxidation.

blocks.title: Coordinate fasting
blocks.text: Glucagon supports hepatic glucose production during fasting. The liver can use glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; fatty-acid oxidation helps supply energy. Muscle glycogen primarily serves muscle rather than directly releasing free glucose into blood.

example.prompt: After a meal, hepatic glycogen synthesis rises. Does that mean all tissues stop oxidizing glucose?
example.reasoning: No. Storage and oxidation can coexist. Hormonal state shifts pathway tendencies, while each tissue continues to meet its own energy needs.

units.prediction: After a meal, hepatic glycogen synthesis rises. Does that mean all tissues stop oxidizing glucose? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: High cellular ATP often signals:
options: An immediate shortage of phosphorylated energy carriers
A signal to accelerate ATP-producing pathways regardless of demand
questions.explanation: High ATP relative to lower-energy adenylates generally signals an energy-rich state and can inhibit ATP-producing pathways. Regulation also depends on tissue, substrate supply, and other signals.

previousVersion.stem: High cellular ATP often signals:
options: Greater immediate need for ATP production
previousVersion.explanation: High ATP relative to low-energy adenylates can signal adequate energy supply.

questions.stem: Which process builds glycogen?
questions.explanation: Glycogenesis synthesizes glycogen from glucose units.

questions.stem: During fasting, glucagon generally promotes hepatic:
options: Conversion of glucose to fatty acids for storage
Glucose oxidation through increased glycolytic flux
questions.explanation: During fasting, glucagon favors hepatic glucose output through glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis. Glycogen and fat storage characterize a different hormonal emphasis.

previousVersion.stem: During fasting, glucagon generally promotes hepatic:
previousVersion.explanation: Glucagon supports hepatic glycogen breakdown and glucose synthesis.

questions.stem: AMP rises as ATP falls in a working cell. This most plausibly signals:
options: An increase in the ATP-to-AMP ratio
A surplus of immediately available ATP
questions.explanation: Rising AMP with falling ATP indicates a lower-energy state and can signal a need for greater ATP regeneration. It is the opposite of an increasing ATP-to-AMP ratio or ATP surplus.

previousVersion.stem: AMP rises as ATP falls in a working cell. This most plausibly signals:
options: A need to stop all catabolism
previousVersion.explanation: AMP can signal a low-energy state and influence energy-producing pathways.

questions.stem: A liver increases gluconeogenesis. It is increasing:
options: Glucose synthesis from suitable noncarbohydrate precursors
Conversion of glucose carbon into fatty acids
questions.explanation: Gluconeogenesis synthesizes glucose from suitable noncarbohydrate precursors. Glycogenolysis releases glucose units from stored glycogen; glycogenesis and fatty-acid synthesis are storage pathways.

previousVersion.stem: A liver increases gluconeogenesis. It is increasing:
options: Glucose synthesis from suitable noncarbohydrate precursors
previousVersion.explanation: Gluconeogenesis forms glucose from precursors such as lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids.

questions.stem: Muscle glycogen is mobilized during exercise. Its primary immediate role is to:
options: Release free glucose directly to maintain systemic blood glucose
Supply the main precursor for ketone production in muscle
Store glucose while avoiding its oxidation during contraction
Supply substrate for the muscle’s own energy use
questions.explanation: Muscle glycogen supplies glucose phosphate for the muscle’s own ATP production. Skeletal muscle lacks the liver’s glucose-6-phosphatase route for exporting large amounts of free glucose; ketogenesis is primarily hepatic.

previousVersion.stem: Muscle glycogen is mobilized during exercise. Its primary immediate role is to:
options: Directly export large amounts of free glucose
Supply substrate for the muscle’s own energy use
previousVersion.explanation: Muscle uses its glycogen locally; it lacks the hepatic mechanism for substantial free-glucose export.

units.title: Copy and repair DNA
units.subtitle: Use directionality to explain leading and lagging synthesis.

blocks.title: Respect directionality
blocks.text: DNA polymerases extend a strand by adding nucleotides to a free 3′ hydroxyl, so new DNA grows 5′ to 3′. The template is read in the opposite direction. A primer provides the initial end.

blocks.title: Resolve antiparallel templates
blocks.text: At a replication fork, one new strand can extend continuously toward fork movement. The other is made in fragments that are later joined. Both strands still grow 5′ to 3′.

blocks.title: Distinguish maintenance tasks
blocks.text: Proofreading can remove a newly misincorporated nucleotide during synthesis. Other repair systems recognize mismatches or damaged bases after synthesis. Repair reduces mutation frequency; it does not guarantee error-free DNA.

example.prompt: A lagging-strand fragment grows away from fork movement. Does it grow 3′ to 5′?
example.reasoning: No. Each fragment is still synthesized 5′ to 3′. Repeated priming accommodates the opposite orientation of the template.

units.prediction: A lagging-strand fragment grows away from fork movement. Does it grow 3′ to 5′? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: New DNA is synthesized in which direction?
options: 3′ to 5′ on the lagging strand and 5′ to 3′ on the leading strand
5′ to 3′ on the lagging strand and 3′ to 5′ on the leading strand
3′ to 5′ on both newly synthesized strands
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase extends the 3′ end, so both leading-strand synthesis and each lagging-strand fragment proceed 5′ to 3′. The antiparallel templates do not reverse the chemistry of nucleotide addition.

previousVersion.stem: New DNA is synthesized in which direction?
previousVersion.explanation: Addition to a free 3′ hydroxyl produces 5′-to-3′ growth.

questions.stem: A primer is needed because DNA polymerase requires:
options: A free 5′ phosphate on the growing strand
An unpaired template base without a paired primer end
A preexisting DNA fragment with no accessible hydroxyl
questions.explanation: Extension requires a primer terminus with a free 3′ hydroxyl. A template alone or a 5′ phosphate does not provide the chemical group needed for that addition.

previousVersion.stem: A primer is needed because DNA polymerase requires:
previousVersion.explanation: The primer supplies an existing 3′ end for extension.

questions.stem: DNA ligase primarily joins:
options: Complementary bases by forming hydrogen bonds
New nucleotides by extending a primer
The two template strands by relieving supercoiling
questions.explanation: DNA ligase seals a nick between adjacent DNA fragments by forming a phosphodiester linkage. It does not replace polymerase-mediated strand extension or topoisomerase-mediated supercoil management.

previousVersion.stem: DNA ligase primarily joins:
previousVersion.explanation: Ligase seals breaks in the sugar-phosphate backbone.

questions.stem: A polymerase adds a labeled nucleotide to a growing strand. The nucleotide is added at its:
options: 5′ end of the newly synthesized strand
questions.explanation: The nucleotide is added to the growing strand’s 3′ hydroxyl. The template directs sequence but is not itself extended by the complementary-strand synthesis step.

previousVersion.stem: A polymerase adds a labeled nucleotide to a growing strand. The nucleotide is added at its:
previousVersion.explanation: DNA extension occurs at the 3′ hydroxyl.

questions.stem: An experiment blocks DNA ligase but allows synthesis. Which material is expected to accumulate?
options: Unwound template DNA with no newly synthesized fragments
Longer continuous lagging strands than in the control
New DNA strands with their primers already replaced and nicks sealed
questions.explanation: Ligase inhibition leaves nicks between newly synthesized fragments, especially on the lagging strand. Ongoing polymerization does not itself seal those nicks or make the discontinuous pathway continuous.

previousVersion.stem: An experiment blocks DNA ligase but allows synthesis. Which material is expected to accumulate?
previousVersion.explanation: Fragments can be synthesized yet remain unsealed.

questions.stem: A proofreading-deficient polymerase most directly increases the chance that:
options: Correctly paired bases are removed more frequently than mismatches
The strands switch their direction of synthesis
Primers are no longer required for strand extension
questions.explanation: Proofreading removes misincorporated nucleotides. Losing it increases persistence of replication errors; it does not eliminate primer requirements or reverse synthesis direction.

previousVersion.stem: A proofreading-deficient polymerase most directly increases the chance that:
previousVersion.explanation: Loss of proofreading allows more synthesis errors to escape immediate correction.

units.title: Follow a gene into a protein
units.subtitle: Separate transcription, RNA processing, and translation.

blocks.title: Identify the template
blocks.text: Transcription produces RNA complementary to a DNA template. The RNA sequence resembles the coding strand, with uracil replacing thymine. RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA 5′ to 3′.

blocks.title: Process the message
blocks.text: In eukaryotic cells, many transcripts undergo capping, splicing, and polyadenylation. Splicing removes introns and joins exons. Alternative splicing can produce different mature RNAs from one gene.

blocks.title: Read a codon
blocks.text: A ribosome reads mRNA codons and incorporates amino acids carried by tRNAs. A frameshift can change downstream codons; a synonymous substitution may preserve the encoded amino acid. Effects depend on position and context.

example.prompt: A DNA coding strand is 5′-ATG GAA-3′. What is the corresponding RNA sequence?
example.reasoning: The RNA is 5′-AUG GAA-3′. It matches the coding strand except U replaces T; the polymerase actually reads the complementary template.

units.prediction: A DNA coding strand is 5′-ATG GAA-3′. What is the corresponding RNA sequence? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Introns are removed during:
questions.explanation: RNA splicing removes introns and joins exons in a pre-mRNA. Transcription creates the RNA, polyadenylation modifies its end, and translation uses mature RNA to produce protein.

previousVersion.stem: Introns are removed during:
previousVersion.explanation: Splicing removes introns from a precursor transcript.

questions.stem: A coding DNA segment 5′-TTC-3′ corresponds to RNA:
questions.explanation: The RNA matches the coding strand’s sequence with U replacing T. Complementing the coding strand instead confuses it with the template; RNA contains U rather than T.

previousVersion.stem: A coding DNA segment 5′-TTC-3′ corresponds to RNA:
previousVersion.explanation: RNA resembles coding DNA with U in place of T.

questions.stem: Removing one nucleotide within a coding region often causes a:
options: Missense substitution without shifting the reading frame
In-frame deletion of a complete codon
questions.explanation: A single-nucleotide deletion in a translated coding sequence shifts downstream codon grouping. Deleting a multiple of three can preserve the frame; substitutions change bases without this deletion-induced shift.

previousVersion.stem: Removing one nucleotide within a coding region often causes a:
previousVersion.explanation: A one-base deletion can shift the triplet reading frame.

questions.stem: Two mature RNAs contain different combinations of exons from the same gene. This is consistent with:
options: A shift in the translation reading frame
A difference in which codons use a particular tRNA
A change in the DNA sequence required for each RNA molecule
questions.explanation: Different exon combinations can result from alternative processing of the same gene’s RNA. No different DNA template or altered genetic code is required; a reading-frame change alone does not explain the exon selection.

previousVersion.stem: Two mature RNAs contain different combinations of exons from the same gene. This is consistent with:
options: Different genetic codes in each exon
previousVersion.explanation: Alternative splicing can join different exon combinations.

questions.stem: A substitution changes a codon but not its amino acid. The coding change is described as:
questions.explanation: A synonymous substitution changes a codon while preserving its encoded amino acid. Missense changes the amino acid, nonsense creates a stop, and frameshift changes downstream codon grouping.

previousVersion.stem: A substitution changes a codon but not its amino acid. The coding change is described as:
previousVersion.explanation: Degeneracy of the genetic code allows different codons to specify the same amino acid.

questions.stem: A treatment reduces translation without changing mRNA abundance. Which measurement may fall directly?
options: The number of copies of the gene
questions.explanation: Translation directly produces new protein. Its inhibition can reduce new protein synthesis even when mRNA abundance is unchanged; DNA copy number and transcription are different processes.

previousVersion.stem: A treatment reduces translation without changing mRNA abundance. Which measurement may fall directly?
options: DNA base number in every cell
previousVersion.explanation: Translation controls protein production from available messages.
