units.title: Reason through inheritance
units.subtitle: Distinguish genotype probability from linkage evidence.

blocks.title: Set up the cross
blocks.text: For an autosomal locus with complete dominance, Aa × Aa gives genotype probabilities 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, and 1/4 aa. Phenotype ratios depend on the dominance model and penetrance assumptions.

blocks.title: Know when to multiply
blocks.text: For independently assorting loci, multiply independent probabilities. Linked loci on one chromosome can violate that independence assumption. A testcross can expose parental and recombinant haplotypes.

blocks.title: Read recombination
blocks.text: For sufficiently close loci, recombination fraction approximates genetic map distance. A fraction near 50% cannot distinguish distant loci on one chromosome from loci on different chromosomes. Multiple crossovers can restore parental marker combinations and make observed recombination underestimate genetic distance. Genetic map distance is not a fixed conversion to physical distance in base pairs.

example.prompt: Independent AaBb parents are crossed. What is the probability of aabb under Mendelian segregation?
example.reasoning: P(aa) = 1/4 and P(bb) = 1/4. Independence allows multiplication: 1/16. Check linkage and inheritance assumptions before using that shortcut.

units.prediction: Independent AaBb parents are crossed. What is the probability of aabb under Mendelian segregation? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: For Aa × Aa, the probability of aa is:
questions.explanation: Each parent transmits a with probability 1/2, giving 1/4.

questions.stem: Independent probabilities 1/4 and 1/4 combine to give:
questions.explanation: Independent joint probability is the product.

questions.stem: A recombination fraction near 50% indicates:
options: The loci are necessarily on different chromosomes
The loci are necessarily far apart on one chromosome
The loci are so close that crossing over is suppressed
No detectable linkage in this cross
questions.explanation: A recombination fraction near 50% shows no detectable linkage in this cross. It does not distinguish loci on different chromosomes from sufficiently distant loci on the same chromosome.

previousVersion.stem: A recombination fraction near 50% indicates:
options: No detectable linkage in this cross
previousVersion.explanation: A value near 50% is compatible with independent assortment or widely separated loci.

questions.stem: An Aa individual is crossed with aa. Under simple Mendelian segregation, the expected Aa fraction is:
questions.explanation: Half the first parent’s gametes carry A; the other parent always supplies a.

questions.stem: A testcross yields 10% recombinant offspring. For closely linked loci, the approximate map distance is:
questions.explanation: For close loci, one percent recombination approximates one centimorgan.

questions.stem: A student multiplies two genotype probabilities despite strong linkage. The calculation may fail because:
options: Linked loci must have identical genotype probabilities
Dominant alleles are transmitted more often than recessive alleles
Linkage guarantees that no recombinant offspring occur
questions.explanation: Multiplying marginal probabilities assumes independence. Linkage can violate that assumption; it neither changes Mendelian dominance into transmission bias nor guarantees zero recombination.

previousVersion.stem: A student multiplies two genotype probabilities despite strong linkage. The calculation may fail because:
previousVersion.explanation: Linkage can make the joint probability differ from the product of marginal probabilities.

units.title: Connect pressure to blood flow
units.subtitle: Use gradients, resistance, and vessel geometry.

blocks.title: Use a pressure difference
blocks.text: Flow depends on the pressure difference across a vascular segment, not on one pressure alone. In a simple steady model, Q = ΔP/R. Raising resistance lowers flow if the pressure difference is held fixed.

blocks.title: Separate flow from speed
blocks.text: Volume flow is volume per time; speed is distance per time. At steady incompressible flow, Q = Av. Blood moves slowly across the enormous total cross-sectional area of the capillary beds.

blocks.title: State the model limits
blocks.text: Ideal laminar tube flow predicts strong radius dependence, R proportional to 1/r⁴. Real vessels are compliant, branching, and actively regulated. The simple relation is most useful when the problem specifies which variables stay fixed.

example.prompt: A vessel’s resistance doubles while its pressure difference stays fixed. What happens to flow?
example.reasoning: From Q = ΔP/R, flow becomes half its original value. This conclusion requires the fixed pressure-difference assumption.

units.prediction: A vessel’s resistance doubles while its pressure difference stays fixed. What happens to flow? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: For fixed ΔP, doubling resistance changes flow to:
questions.explanation: Flow is inversely proportional to resistance at fixed pressure difference.

questions.stem: Volume flow equals:
questions.explanation: Volume per time equals cross-sectional area times mean speed. Dividing these terms produces different units, and the pressure–flow relation divides pressure difference by resistance rather than multiplying.

previousVersion.stem: Volume flow equals:
previousVersion.explanation: Q = Av for incompressible steady flow.

questions.stem: Capillary-bed speed is low partly because total cross-sectional area is:
options: Smaller than the total area of the supplying arteries
Equal to the area of a single capillary
Constant regardless of the number of parallel capillaries
questions.explanation: For the same total volume flow, speed falls as total cross-sectional area rises. The relevant area sums the many parallel capillaries rather than using the area of just one vessel.

previousVersion.stem: Capillary-bed speed is low partly because total cross-sectional area is:
previousVersion.explanation: At the same total flow, a larger total area implies lower mean speed.

questions.stem: ΔP rises from 40 to 60 units while resistance is unchanged. Flow rises by a factor of:
questions.explanation: At fixed resistance, flow is proportional to ΔP: 60/40 = 1.5.

questions.stem: A cylindrical tube radius doubles under ideal laminar conditions, with length and viscosity fixed. Its resistance changes by a factor of:
questions.explanation: Resistance scales as r to the minus fourth power.

questions.stem: Two segments have the same upstream pressure but different downstream pressures. To compare flow, first compare:
options: Their upstream pressures without their downstream pressures
Their downstream pressures without their resistances
Their lengths without considering their radii or viscosity
questions.explanation: Flow depends on pressure difference divided by resistance. Either endpoint pressure alone misses the driving difference; length alone does not specify resistance.

previousVersion.stem: Two segments have the same upstream pressure but different downstream pressures. To compare flow, first compare:
previousVersion.explanation: Flow depends on the pressure drop across each segment and its resistance.

units.title: Move oxygen across a barrier
units.subtitle: Connect partial pressure, diffusion, and hemoglobin.

blocks.title: Follow partial pressure
blocks.text: A gas diffuses down its partial-pressure gradient. Across the respiratory membrane, oxygen normally moves from alveolar air toward blood, while carbon dioxide moves in the opposite direction.

blocks.title: Change the barrier
blocks.text: Diffusion is favored by greater surface area and a larger driving gradient, and hindered by a thicker barrier. Different gases also differ in solubility and diffusivity.

blocks.title: Distinguish pressure from content
blocks.text: Dissolved oxygen contributes to partial pressure. Hemoglobin-bound oxygen contributes substantially to oxygen content without directly determining dissolved partial pressure. A reduction in hemoglobin can lower oxygen content even when partial pressure is preserved.

example.prompt: Two blood samples have similar oxygen partial pressures but different hemoglobin concentrations. Must their oxygen contents match?
example.reasoning: No. Oxygen content includes the amount bound to hemoglobin. The sample with less hemoglobin can carry less total oxygen despite a similar partial pressure.

units.prediction: Two blood samples have similar oxygen partial pressures but different hemoglobin concentrations. Must their oxygen contents match? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Gas diffusion is directly driven by a difference in:
options: Total gas pressure regardless of composition
Hemoglobin saturation independently of dissolved gas
Oxygen content independently of dissolved gas
questions.explanation: For a given gas, partial-pressure difference drives net diffusion. Oxygen content and hemoglobin saturation can change without an equivalent change in dissolved-gas partial pressure.

previousVersion.stem: Gas diffusion is directly driven by a difference in:
previousVersion.explanation: A partial-pressure gradient provides the driving force for gas diffusion.

questions.stem: Doubling barrier thickness, with other ideal diffusion factors fixed, should:
options: Leave the rate unchanged because the pressure difference persists
questions.explanation: In the ideal diffusion relation, rate is inversely proportional to barrier thickness. Doubling thickness halves the rate when area, diffusion coefficient, and partial-pressure difference are fixed.

previousVersion.stem: Doubling barrier thickness, with other ideal diffusion factors fixed, should:
previousVersion.explanation: A thicker diffusion path slows transfer under the simple diffusion relation.

questions.stem: Reduced hemoglobin with preserved dissolved oxygen can lower:
options: Arterial oxygen partial pressure despite unchanged dissolved oxygen
questions.explanation: Oxygen content includes hemoglobin-bound oxygen, so lowering hemoglobin can reduce content even when dissolved oxygen and its partial pressure are preserved.

previousVersion.stem: Reduced hemoglobin with preserved dissolved oxygen can lower:
options: All oxygen partial pressures to zero
previousVersion.explanation: Less hemoglobin reduces oxygen-carrying capacity even if dissolved oxygen is similar.

questions.stem: A model doubles exchange area without changing thickness or gradient. Predicted diffusion rate:
questions.explanation: Rate is proportional to exchange area in the ideal diffusion model.

questions.stem: Alveolar oxygen partial pressure exceeds capillary oxygen partial pressure. Initial net oxygen movement is toward:
options: Neither compartment until their pressures are equal
Both directions at equal rates despite the pressure difference
questions.explanation: Net diffusion is from the higher alveolar oxygen partial pressure toward the lower capillary value. Molecules move both ways, but the unequal driving forces give an initial net movement into blood.

previousVersion.stem: Alveolar oxygen partial pressure exceeds capillary oxygen partial pressure. Initial net oxygen movement is toward:
previousVersion.explanation: Oxygen moves down its partial-pressure gradient into blood.

questions.stem: A report treats oxygen saturation and oxygen content as identical quantities. The missing consideration is:
options: Atmospheric pressure as a substitute for hemoglobin concentration
Heart rate as a substitute for hemoglobin concentration
Blood pH as a complete measure of oxygen-carrying capacity
questions.explanation: Saturation is the fraction of hemoglobin binding sites occupied. Content also depends on how much hemoglobin is present, plus dissolved oxygen; equal saturation can accompany different oxygen contents.

previousVersion.stem: A report treats oxygen saturation and oxygen content as identical quantities. The missing consideration is:
previousVersion.explanation: At the same saturation, oxygen content varies with the amount of hemoglobin.

units.title: Regulate water in the nephron
units.subtitle: Distinguish filtration, reabsorption, secretion, and excretion.

blocks.title: Track a substance
blocks.text: Filtration moves material from plasma into the nephron. Reabsorption returns it to blood; secretion moves it from blood into tubular fluid. Excretion equals filtration minus reabsorption plus secretion for a substance in this accounting model.

blocks.title: Read the water gradient
blocks.text: The kidney can conserve water when collecting ducts are water-permeable and a suitable medullary osmotic gradient exists. ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin regulation.

blocks.title: Predict a paired change
blocks.text: With other conditions suitable, more ADH favors more water reabsorption, lower urine volume, and more concentrated urine. A damaged osmotic gradient can limit this effect even when the hormonal signal is present.

example.prompt: ADH rises, but the medullary concentration gradient is lost. Is strong water conservation guaranteed?
example.reasoning: No. Permeability alone is insufficient: an osmotic driving force is also needed. Keep the barrier and the gradient separate.

units.prediction: ADH rises, but the medullary concentration gradient is lost. Is strong water conservation guaranteed? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Moving a filtered solute from tubular fluid back to blood is:
questions.explanation: Reabsorption returns material from the tubule to the circulation.

questions.stem: ADH typically increases collecting-duct permeability to:
questions.explanation: ADH promotes aquaporin-mediated water permeability in the collecting duct. Aquaporins are water channels; they do not carry sodium, glucose, or albumin.

previousVersion.stem: ADH typically increases collecting-duct permeability to:
previousVersion.explanation: ADH regulates aquaporins that increase water permeability.

questions.stem: A substance has filtration of 100 mg/min, reabsorption of 80 mg/min, and secretion of 5 mg/min. Its excretion rate in mg/min is:
questions.explanation: Use the substance balance: excretion = filtration − reabsorption + secretion = 100 − 80 + 5 = 25, in the same amount-per-time units.

questions.stem: A substance is filtered and fully reabsorbed without secretion. Its excretion is:
options: Equal to the filtered plus reabsorbed amounts
questions.explanation: Excretion equals filtration minus reabsorption plus secretion. Complete reabsorption with no secretion leaves none of this filtered substance to be excreted.

previousVersion.stem: A substance is filtered and fully reabsorbed without secretion. Its excretion is:
previousVersion.explanation: Complete reabsorption returns all filtered material under the stated assumptions.

questions.stem: ADH increases with an intact medullary gradient. Urine volume is expected to:
options: Remain unchanged while urine concentration rises
Increase because collecting-duct water permeability falls
questions.explanation: With an intact osmotic gradient, ADH increases water reabsorption and tends to reduce urine volume while concentrating the urine. Reabsorption returns water to blood rather than adding it to urine.

previousVersion.stem: ADH increases with an intact medullary gradient. Urine volume is expected to:
previousVersion.explanation: Greater water reabsorption tends to reduce excreted water volume.

questions.stem: Aquaporins are present, but little osmotic gradient remains. Water reabsorption may be limited by:
options: The size of the filtered sodium load alone
The number of aquaporins regardless of the gradient
The rate of water pumping by aquaporins
questions.explanation: Water channels provide permeability but do not actively pump water. A weak osmotic gradient can limit net reabsorption even when channels are present.

previousVersion.stem: Aquaporins are present, but little osmotic gradient remains. Water reabsorption may be limited by:
options: A lack of amino acids in urine
previousVersion.explanation: Channels enable movement, but net movement also requires a gradient.

units.title: Compare molecules in three dimensions
units.subtitle: Identify connectivity, mirror relationships, and stereocenters.

blocks.title: Compare connectivity first
blocks.text: Isomers share a molecular formula. Constitutional isomers differ in which atoms are connected; stereoisomers share connectivity but differ in spatial arrangement. A tetrahedral carbon bearing four different substituents is a common stereogenic center.

blocks.title: Test the mirror relationship
blocks.text: Enantiomers are nonsuperimposable mirror images. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images. A molecule with stereocenters can still be achiral when symmetry makes the whole molecule superimposable on its mirror image.

blocks.title: Keep labels distinct
blocks.text: R and S specify configuration under priority rules; they do not by themselves predict the sign of optical rotation. Biological binding sites are chiral and may interact differently with enantiomers.

example.prompt: Two molecules share connectivity but differ at one of two stereocenters while matching at the other. What relationship is expected?
example.reasoning: They are diastereomers, assuming they are distinct molecules. Enantiomers would invert all stereocenters in this simple comparison.

units.prediction: Two molecules share connectivity but differ at one of two stereocenters while matching at the other. What relationship is expected? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Molecules with the same molecular formula but different atom connectivity are:
questions.explanation: Constitutional isomers share a molecular formula but differ in connectivity. Conformational changes, enantiomers, and diastereomers preserve connectivity.

previousVersion.stem: Molecules with the same molecular formula but different atom connectivity are:
previousVersion.explanation: Constitutional isomers have the same molecular formula but differ in atom connectivity. Different connectivity alone does not establish isomerism without a shared formula.

questions.stem: Nonsuperimposable mirror-image molecules are:
questions.explanation: Nonsuperimposable mirror images are enantiomers. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images; constitutional isomers change connectivity, while resonance contributors do not represent separate molecules.

previousVersion.stem: Nonsuperimposable mirror-image molecules are:
previousVersion.explanation: This is the defining relationship of enantiomers.

questions.stem: R configuration alone tells you the sign of optical rotation:
options: It does not determine the sign
questions.explanation: Absolute configuration and measured rotation sign are different descriptors.

questions.stem: Two distinct molecules share connectivity and have two stereocenters. They match at one center and differ at the other. In this comparison they are:
questions.explanation: They are stereoisomers without a complete mirror relationship.

questions.stem: A tetrahedral carbon is bonded to H, H, Br, and CH3. It is not stereogenic because:
options: The carbon is tetrahedral rather than planar
The substituents contain atoms with different masses
questions.explanation: A tetrahedral carbon needs four different substituents to be a stereogenic center of this type. Two identical hydrogens prevent that distinction; hydrogen or tetrahedral geometry alone does not.

previousVersion.stem: A tetrahedral carbon is bonded to H, H, Br, and CH3. It is not stereogenic because:
previousVersion.explanation: A simple tetrahedral stereocenter requires four different substituents.

questions.stem: Two enantiomers bind differently to an enzyme. A relevant explanation is that the active site:
options: Gives the two enantiomers different molecular formulas
Makes the free enantiomers have different molecular masses
Must bind both enantiomers in identical orientations
questions.explanation: An enzyme’s chiral binding environment can make different interactions with two enantiomers. Their formulas and masses remain the same, but equivalent fitting orientations are not guaranteed.

previousVersion.stem: Two enantiomers bind differently to an enzyme. A relevant explanation is that the active site:
previousVersion.explanation: A chiral binding environment can distinguish mirror-image ligands.

units.title: Follow electrons at a carbonyl
units.subtitle: Use polarity and leaving groups to distinguish reaction paths.

blocks.title: Find the electrophile
blocks.text: The C=O bond is polarized toward oxygen, making carbonyl carbon electrophilic. A nucleophile supplies an electron pair to form a bond; curved arrows begin at an electron source.

blocks.title: Follow the intermediate
blocks.text: Nucleophilic attack on a carbonyl can produce a tetrahedral intermediate. Aldehydes and ketones commonly undergo addition. Acyl derivatives can undergo substitution when the intermediate can expel a suitable leaving group.

blocks.title: Check conditions
blocks.text: Protonation can activate a carbonyl or improve a leaving group. Solvent, acid–base state, steric effects, and leaving-group ability affect a proposed mechanism. Avoid applying a reaction label without checking the substrate.

example.prompt: Why does a nucleophile commonly attack carbonyl carbon rather than carbonyl oxygen?
example.reasoning: Carbonyl carbon is electron-poor because oxygen attracts electron density. The nucleophile donates a pair toward that electrophilic center.

units.prediction: Why does a nucleophile commonly attack carbonyl carbon rather than carbonyl oxygen? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: At a typical carbonyl, the electrophilic atom is:
questions.explanation: C=O polarization leaves the carbon relatively electron-poor.

questions.stem: In a two-electron polar mechanism, a full-headed curved arrow should begin at:
options: An electron-deficient atom that will accept the pair
The positive formal charge on the electrophile
The destination atom before its bond is formed
questions.explanation: A full-headed arrow starts at the electron source, a lone pair or bond, and points toward its destination. Starting at the electrophile reverses this convention; half-headed arrows denote single electrons.

previousVersion.stem: In a two-electron polar mechanism, a full-headed curved arrow should begin at:
options: A positive sign with no electrons
previousVersion.explanation: A full-headed curved arrow follows an electron pair from a lone pair or bond to its destination. Half-headed fishhook arrows instead represent single-electron movement.

questions.stem: Acyl substitution differs from simple addition because it includes:
options: Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen as its defining step
Permanent loss of the carbonyl double bond
Formation of a new carbon stereocenter in every case
questions.explanation: Nucleophilic acyl substitution includes departure of a leaving group and typically restores the carbonyl. Protonation can occur in either pathway and is not the defining distinction; addition need not create a stereocenter.

previousVersion.stem: Acyl substitution differs from simple addition because it includes:
previousVersion.explanation: The tetrahedral intermediate can collapse while expelling a leaving group.

questions.stem: An electron-rich reagent donates a pair to a carbonyl carbon. It acts as a:
questions.explanation: The electron-pair donor is a nucleophile, also acting as a Lewis base. The carbonyl carbon accepts the pair; a Lewis acid accepts rather than donates it.

previousVersion.stem: An electron-rich reagent donates a pair to a carbonyl carbon. It acts as a:
previousVersion.explanation: The reagent supplies the pair forming the new bond.

questions.stem: An aldehyde undergoes hydride addition followed by protonation. The carbonyl becomes an:
questions.explanation: Hydride addition reduces an aldehyde carbonyl; protonation of the resulting alkoxide gives an alcohol. The sequence does not introduce the connectivity of an ester or ether or oxidize the aldehyde to an acid.

previousVersion.stem: An aldehyde undergoes hydride addition followed by protonation. The carbonyl becomes an:
previousVersion.explanation: Hydride addition reduces the aldehyde carbonyl to a primary alcohol after workup.

questions.stem: A proposed acyl-substitution mechanism omits any group that can leave. The key issue is:
options: Whether the substrate’s carbonyl oxygen has lone pairs
Whether the nucleophile can donate an electron pair
Whether the reaction medium can transfer protons
Whether the substrate can support substitution rather than addition
questions.explanation: For substitution, an added group must ultimately replace a group that can depart. Electron donation, oxygen lone pairs, or proton transfer alone do not supply the missing leaving-group pathway.

previousVersion.stem: A proposed acyl-substitution mechanism omits any group that can leave. The key issue is:
options: Whether carbon has an atomic number
Whether arrows can ever be used
Whether the substrate can support substitution rather than addition
previousVersion.explanation: Substitution requires a route for replacing a substituent; substrate structure matters.

units.title: Choose a separation method
units.subtitle: Connect polarity, charge, size, and measurement.

blocks.title: Use a chemical difference
blocks.text: Extraction separates compounds by partition between phases. Acid–base treatment can change a compound’s charge and therefore its phase preference. State which layer contains the species under the given conditions.

blocks.title: Read chromatography
blocks.text: In normal-phase chromatography with a polar stationary phase, stronger stationary-phase interaction usually slows movement. Thin-layer Rf is distance traveled by the analyte divided by distance traveled by the solvent front.

blocks.title: Identify what is measured
blocks.text: A separation signal alone does not establish molecular identity or purity under every condition. Compare standards or use complementary methods. Distillation instead exploits differences in volatility, with behavior affected by pressure and mixture composition.

example.prompt: On a TLC plate a spot travels 3 cm and the solvent front travels 6 cm. What is Rf?
example.reasoning: Rf = 3/6 = 0.50. Both distances share units, so the ratio is dimensionless.

units.prediction: On a TLC plate a spot travels 3 cm and the solvent front travels 6 cm. What is Rf? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: A TLC Rf value is:
questions.explanation: Rf is the spot’s travel from the origin divided by the solvent front’s travel from that same origin. Inverting the ratio, using total plate length, or subtracting distances does not give Rf.

previousVersion.stem: A TLC Rf value is:
previousVersion.explanation: Rf compares two distances measured from the origin.

questions.stem: In normal-phase TLC, stronger interaction with polar silica usually gives:
options: More travel because adsorption favors the mobile phase
The same travel because molecular mass is unchanged
A higher Rf because retention on silica is stronger
Less travel under the same conditions
questions.explanation: Stronger retention by the polar stationary phase reduces migration under otherwise matched normal-phase TLC conditions. Rf therefore falls; stronger adsorption does not favor the mobile phase.

previousVersion.stem: In normal-phase TLC, stronger interaction with polar silica usually gives:
options: Less travel under the same conditions
previousVersion.explanation: Retention by the stationary phase slows movement.

questions.stem: Converting a neutral organic acid to its ionic salt often increases its preference for:
options: A nonpolar organic phase over water
The organic phase because charge is neutralized by the counterion
Neither phase because forming a salt prevents solvation
questions.explanation: Ionization often increases aqueous solubility through favorable interactions with water. The counterion does not make the salt behave as the neutral organic acid; actual partitioning still depends on solvent and structure.

previousVersion.stem: Converting a neutral organic acid to its ionic salt often increases its preference for:
previousVersion.explanation: Ionization often favors interaction with water; actual partition also depends on structure and conditions.

questions.stem: A spot moves 2 cm while the solvent front moves 8 cm. Rf is:
questions.explanation: Measure both distances from the origin. Rf = 2 cm / 8 cm = 0.25. The units cancel; dividing by spot distance would invert the definition.

questions.stem: A method separates liquids primarily by volatility. It is:
questions.explanation: Distillation exploits differences in volatility. Filtration separates particles from fluid, extraction uses partitioning, and size-exclusion chromatography separates by access to pores.

previousVersion.stem: A method separates liquids primarily by volatility. It is:
previousVersion.explanation: Distillation uses vapor–liquid behavior and volatility differences.

questions.stem: Two compounds share a TLC Rf in one solvent. This alone proves:
options: Only that they comigrate in those conditions
questions.explanation: Different compounds can comigrate; additional evidence is needed for identity.

units.title: Choose a force or energy model
units.subtitle: Recognize which conservation statement applies.

blocks.title: Start with the system
blocks.text: Newton’s second law relates net force to mass times acceleration. A force diagram makes the chosen system and directions explicit. Forces on different objects do not belong in one object’s net-force sum.

blocks.title: Track work and energy
blocks.text: Net work equals change in kinetic energy. For a constant force, W = Fd cos θ. Mechanical energy is conserved when only conservative forces do work; friction can transfer mechanical energy into thermal energy.

blocks.title: Use proportional reasoning
blocks.text: Kinetic energy is 1/2 mv². Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy at fixed mass. Momentum is mv, so the same speed change only doubles momentum. Identify the requested quantity before using a proportional shortcut.

example.prompt: A cart doubles its speed at fixed mass. How do kinetic energy and momentum change?
example.reasoning: Kinetic energy becomes four times larger because it depends on v². Momentum doubles because it depends linearly on v.

units.prediction: A cart doubles its speed at fixed mass. How do kinetic energy and momentum change? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Net work equals the change in:
questions.explanation: The net-work theorem relates net work to change in kinetic energy. Work by a particular conservative force can be related to potential energy, but net work is not generally a change in momentum or total mechanical energy.

previousVersion.stem: Net work equals the change in:
previousVersion.explanation: The work–energy theorem relates net work to change in kinetic energy.

questions.stem: Doubling speed at fixed mass multiplies kinetic energy by:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy scales with the square of speed.

questions.stem: A force perpendicular to displacement does constant-force work equal to:
questions.explanation: For a constant force, work is Fd cos θ. At 90 degrees the cosine is zero, regardless of the force magnitude; positive or negative Fd corresponds to parallel or antiparallel force.

previousVersion.stem: A force perpendicular to displacement does constant-force work equal to:
previousVersion.explanation: cos 90° = 0, so the work is zero.

questions.stem: A 2 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². Net force is:
questions.explanation: Newton’s second law gives net force: Fnet = ma = 2 kg × 3 m/s² = 6 N. The product has units of force; this is the sum of forces on the object.

questions.stem: Friction slows a block sliding along a level surface without appreciable elastic deformation. Its lost mechanical energy can appear as:
options: Gravitational potential energy of the block
Energy permanently removed from the block–surface system
Elastic potential energy stored entirely in the block
questions.explanation: Friction can convert mechanical energy into thermal energy of the block and surface. On a level surface the height does not increase, and the loss of mechanical energy is not destruction of total energy.

previousVersion.stem: Friction slows a sliding block. Its lost mechanical energy can appear as:
previousVersion.explanation: Energy transfers into microscopic motion and other forms; total energy remains conserved.

questions.stem: At fixed mass, tripling speed multiplies momentum by:
questions.explanation: Momentum is linear in speed: p = mv.

units.title: Read pressure in a fluid
units.subtitle: Separate depth pressure from buoyant force.

blocks.title: Follow depth
blocks.text: For a constant-density fluid at rest, pressure increases with depth by ρgh. Pressure is force per area; it is not the same as the total force on a surface.

blocks.title: Use displaced volume
blocks.text: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid. A fully submerged object displaces its own volume. Whether it rises or sinks depends on how buoyant force compares with its weight and other applied forces.

blocks.title: Keep assumptions visible
blocks.text: The simple depth relation assumes static fluid and approximately constant density. Gauge pressure excludes the reference atmospheric pressure; absolute pressure includes it. Choose the pressure type requested by the problem.

example.prompt: Two points lie at the same depth in connected, static water. Must the container widths be equal for their pressures to match?
example.reasoning: No. Under the static constant-density assumptions, pressure at a given depth depends on reference pressure, density, and depth, not container width.

units.prediction: Two points lie at the same depth in connected, static water. Must the container widths be equal for their pressures to match? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Hydrostatic pressure change with depth is:
questions.explanation: For a static fluid of constant density, the pressure increase over depth h is ρgh. Adding atmospheric pressure gives absolute pressure; the speed-dependent term belongs to flow, not hydrostatic depth.

previousVersion.stem: Hydrostatic pressure change with depth is:

questions.stem: Gauge pressure is absolute pressure minus:
options: The pressure added by the fluid column
The pressure at the bottom of the container
The dynamic pressure from fluid speed

previousVersion.stem: Gauge pressure is absolute pressure minus:
previousVersion.explanation: Gauge pressure is measured relative to the atmospheric reference.

units.title: Follow flow through a narrowing
units.subtitle: Use continuity and resistance without mixing assumptions.

blocks.title: Conserve volume flow
blocks.text: For steady incompressible flow through an unbranched tube, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. A smaller cross-sectional area requires greater speed when the same volume flow passes through.

blocks.title: Read a pressure relation
blocks.text: Bernoulli’s relation connects pressure, kinetic energy per volume, and gravitational energy per volume under ideal flow assumptions. At the same height, higher speed can accompany lower static pressure along a streamline.

blocks.title: Model viscous resistance
blocks.text: Poiseuille’s relation gives Q proportional to ΔP r⁴/(ηL) for steady laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a cylindrical tube. Radius, viscosity, and length must be distinguished. Do not combine fixed-flow and fixed-pressure assumptions inadvertently.

example.prompt: A tube radius halves while ΔP, viscosity, and length stay fixed under Poiseuille conditions. What happens to flow?
example.reasoning: Flow becomes (1/2)⁴ = 1/16 of its former value. A continuity question that holds flow fixed would describe different constraints.

units.prediction: A tube radius halves while ΔP, viscosity, and length stay fixed under Poiseuille conditions. What happens to flow? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: For steady incompressible flow, Av represents:
questions.explanation: Cross-sectional area times mean speed has dimensions of volume per time. Multiplying by density would give mass flow rate; area times speed is neither speed alone nor resistance.

previousVersion.stem: For steady incompressible flow, Av represents:
previousVersion.explanation: Cross-sectional area times speed gives volume per time.

questions.stem: Halving area at fixed volume flow changes speed by a factor of:
questions.explanation: To preserve Av, speed must double.

questions.stem: At fixed pressure difference, viscosity, and tube length, doubling radius in Poiseuille flow changes Q by:
questions.explanation: Q scales with the fourth power of radius.

questions.stem: Viscosity doubles with other Poiseuille variables fixed. Flow becomes:
questions.explanation: Flow is inversely proportional to viscosity.

questions.stem: A horizontal ideal streamline speeds up. Bernoulli’s relation predicts static pressure tends to:
options: Remain constant because the streamline is horizontal
Require viscosity data before any direction can be predicted
Increase as the kinetic-energy term increases
questions.explanation: Along the specified ideal horizontal streamline, static pressure plus one-half ρv² is constant. A speed increase raises the kinetic term and lowers static pressure; height constancy does not mean pressure constancy.

previousVersion.stem: A horizontal ideal streamline speeds up. Bernoulli’s relation predicts static pressure tends to:
previousVersion.explanation: An increase in kinetic energy per volume can come with a decrease in static pressure.

questions.stem: A narrowed tube has fixed pressure difference, not fixed flow. Assuming its speed must double solely from continuity ignores:
options: That continuity requires the same speed at every cross-section
That pressure difference and volume flow are interchangeable constraints
That the radius alone fixes speed independently of resistance
questions.explanation: Continuity relates speed to area for the actual volume flow. At fixed pressure difference, changing resistance can change that flow, so one cannot assume the original flow value remains fixed.

previousVersion.stem: A narrowed tube has fixed pressure difference, not fixed flow. Assuming its speed must double solely from continuity ignores:
previousVersion.explanation: Continuity relates local quantities within the same flow; it does not force two different operating conditions to have the same Q.

units.title: From stimulus to perception
units.subtitle: Separate transduction, adaptation, and interpretation.

blocks.title: Convert a stimulus
blocks.text: Sensory transduction converts stimulus energy into cellular signals. Different receptors respond to different forms of energy, such as light, mechanical deformation, or chemicals.

blocks.title: Distinguish detection from meaning
blocks.text: Sensation concerns detection and early encoding; perception concerns organization and interpretation. Bottom-up processing begins with incoming information. Top-down influences include expectations, context, and prior knowledge.

blocks.title: Interpret adaptation
blocks.text: A sustained stimulus can produce a reduced sensory response over time. Adaptation is not the same as forgetting or a deliberate change in response strategy. The mechanism depends on the sensory system.

example.prompt: A constant odor becomes less noticeable while its concentration remains stable. What process may contribute?
example.reasoning: Sensory adaptation may reduce responsiveness to sustained stimulation. This observation alone does not identify the precise receptor or neural mechanism.

units.prediction: A constant odor becomes less noticeable while its concentration remains stable. What process may contribute? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Converting light into a receptor signal is:
questions.explanation: Transduction converts stimulus energy into a physiological receptor signal. Adaptation concerns changing sensitivity over time; perceptual organization and response selection occur beyond the initial conversion.

previousVersion.stem: Converting light into a receptor signal is:
previousVersion.explanation: Transduction changes stimulus energy into a biological signal.

questions.stem: Expectations influencing interpretation illustrate:
questions.explanation: Expectations supply prior knowledge that shapes interpretation, an example of top-down processing. They need not change physical stimulus intensity or receptor adaptation.

previousVersion.stem: Expectations influencing interpretation illustrate:
previousVersion.explanation: Prior knowledge and expectations can shape perception.

questions.stem: A decreasing response to a sustained stimulus is compatible with:
options: An increase in receptor response gain
questions.explanation: Adaptation is a reduced response during sustained stimulation. Sensitization or increased gain predicts greater responsiveness; the statement does not report a growing physical stimulus.

previousVersion.stem: A decreasing response to a sustained stimulus is compatible with:
previousVersion.explanation: Sensory systems can reduce responses during continued stimulation.

questions.stem: Using local edges to build a visual representation emphasizes:
questions.explanation: Constructing a representation from stimulus features emphasizes bottom-up processing. Context, expectations, and prior hypotheses describe top-down influences instead.

previousVersion.stem: Using local edges to build a visual representation emphasizes:
previousVersion.explanation: The representation is built from incoming sensory features.

questions.stem: A sentence makes an ambiguous word easier to identify. The sentence provides:
options: An increase in the word’s physical contrast
An increase in peripheral receptor sensitivity
A longer-lasting sensory trace by definition
questions.explanation: The sentence adds meaning and expectations that can guide identification. Better identification alone does not establish changed contrast, receptor sensitivity, or sensory-storage duration.

previousVersion.stem: A sentence makes an ambiguous word easier to identify. The sentence provides:
previousVersion.explanation: Context constrains interpretation using knowledge beyond the isolated stimulus.

questions.stem: A researcher measures receptor voltage after a mechanical deflection. This directly studies:
options: Long-term potentiation of a memory circuit
A decision criterion for reporting a stimulus
questions.explanation: Relating physical deflection to receptor voltage directly examines conversion of mechanical stimulation into an electrical signal. It is not itself a measure of memory change or a conscious reporting criterion.

previousVersion.stem: A researcher measures receptor voltage after a mechanical deflection. This directly studies:
previousVersion.explanation: The experiment links physical stimulation to an electrical receptor response.

units.title: Separate sensitivity from response bias
units.subtitle: Read thresholds, proportional changes, and decisions.

blocks.title: Define a threshold
blocks.text: An absolute threshold is conventionally the stimulus level detected on half of trials under specified conditions. A difference threshold concerns the smallest reliably detectable change between stimuli.

blocks.title: Use Weber’s relation
blocks.text: Over suitable ranges, the just-noticeable difference can be approximately proportional to initial stimulus intensity. The ratio ΔI/I is then approximately constant, rather than the absolute change remaining constant.

blocks.title: Separate decision from detection
blocks.text: Signal detection theory distinguishes sensitivity from response criterion. A more liberal criterion can increase both hits and false alarms without improved sensory sensitivity. Evaluate both outcomes rather than only hit rate.

example.prompt: A warning encourages participants to report faint tones more often. Hits and false alarms both rise. Must sensitivity have improved?
example.reasoning: No. The pattern can follow a more liberal response criterion. Hit rate alone cannot isolate sensitivity.

units.prediction: A warning encourages participants to report faint tones more often. Hits and false alarms both rise. Must sensitivity have improved? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: A more liberal response criterion can increase:
questions.explanation: A more liberal criterion favors reporting signal present: hits and false alarms can rise, while misses and correct rejections fall. The criterion shift does not itself establish improved sensitivity.

previousVersion.stem: A more liberal response criterion can increase:
previousVersion.explanation: A lower threshold for saying yes can increase both response types.

questions.stem: Weber’s law approximately keeps which ratio constant?
questions.explanation: Weber’s law approximates a constant detectable increment relative to baseline intensity, ΔI/I. Multiplying by intensity or squaring one term gives a different scaling rule.

previousVersion.stem: Weber’s law approximately keeps which ratio constant?
previousVersion.explanation: The noticeable change scales with baseline intensity in the applicable range.

questions.stem: An absolute threshold conventionally corresponds to detection on approximately:
questions.explanation: The conventional threshold is the level detected half the time under specified conditions.

questions.stem: If a 10-unit stimulus needs a 1-unit change, Weber scaling predicts a 30-unit stimulus needs about:
questions.explanation: The fraction is 0.1; 0.1 × 30 = 3.

questions.stem: A participant reports a signal when none was present. This is a:
questions.explanation: A yes response on a noise-only trial is a false alarm.

questions.stem: A study reports only hits while omitting false alarms. It cannot cleanly distinguish improved sensitivity from:
options: A reduction in both hits and false alarms
A lower reporting rate in signal-present trials
A decrease in response bias toward reporting a signal
questions.explanation: A liberal criterion can raise hits and false alarms without better discrimination. Hit rate alone cannot separate that bias from increased sensitivity; the missing false-alarm information is essential.

previousVersion.stem: A study reports only hits while omitting false alarms. It cannot cleanly distinguish improved sensitivity from:
previousVersion.explanation: Both sensitivity and response criterion can affect hit rate.

units.title: Allocate attention
units.subtitle: Connect selection, interference, and task demands.

blocks.title: Select among inputs
blocks.text: Selective attention prioritizes some information over other information. Divided attention distributes resources across tasks; demanding tasks can interfere with one another.

blocks.title: Read an interference effect
blocks.text: In a Stroop-style task, automatic word reading can interfere with naming ink color. Longer response time under incongruent conditions supports competition between relevant and irrelevant processing, within the task’s design.

blocks.title: Use a careful claim
blocks.text: Poor recall for an unattended stimulus does not prove that no processing occurred. A behavioral measure samples one outcome. Compare appropriate control conditions and distinguish response accuracy from response time.

example.prompt: Ink-color naming is slower for incongruent words than neutral strings. What does the comparison suggest?
example.reasoning: Processing the word can interfere with the instructed color response. The result does not establish that every unattended stimulus receives complete semantic analysis.

units.prediction: Ink-color naming is slower for incongruent words than neutral strings. What does the comparison suggest? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Prioritizing one conversation in a crowded room illustrates:
questions.explanation: Selecting one stream from competing conversations illustrates selective attention. Dividing attention across streams and sustaining attention over time describe different demands.

previousVersion.stem: Prioritizing one conversation in a crowded room illustrates:
previousVersion.explanation: Attention selects relevant information among competing inputs.

questions.stem: A Stroop interference effect commonly involves conflict between:
options: Naming the meaning of a color word and ignoring its sound
Repeating a color name and retaining it in working memory
Detecting ink brightness and identifying font size
questions.explanation: The classic Stroop task requires naming ink color while resisting the competing response elicited by reading an incongruent color word. The interference is not primarily a brightness, font-size, or verbal-retention comparison.

previousVersion.stem: A Stroop interference effect commonly involves conflict between:
previousVersion.explanation: The automatic reading response can compete with the required color response.

questions.stem: Doing two demanding tasks at once can impair performance because:
options: Practice necessarily transfers from one task to the other
Both tasks receive the full resources available during single-task performance
The tasks become less demanding simply because they occur together
questions.explanation: Two demanding tasks can compete for limited processing resources. Simultaneous performance does not guarantee automaticity, positive transfer, or full single-task resources for both.

previousVersion.stem: Doing two demanding tasks at once can impair performance because:
previousVersion.explanation: Tasks can compete for limited processing resources.

questions.stem: A participant is accurate but slower in one condition. A complete comparison should retain:
options: The number of trials without either performance measure
questions.explanation: Accuracy and latency capture different aspects of performance and potential tradeoffs. Keeping only one can hide the cost associated with the other.

previousVersion.stem: A participant is accurate but slower in one condition. A complete comparison should retain:
previousVersion.explanation: Speed–accuracy differences can be lost when only one measure is considered.

questions.stem: No later recall for an unattended word proves:
options: Only that recall was not demonstrated by that test
questions.explanation: A failed memory measure does not establish absence of all earlier processing.

questions.stem: To assess interference, compare an incongruent condition with:
options: The incongruent condition repeated with fewer response options
An unrelated task performed by a different group
An appropriate neutral or congruent control
A condition with different stimuli and a different required response
questions.explanation: A suitable neutral or congruent comparison helps isolate the interference-producing feature while matching other demands. Changing the task, response set, or population introduces alternative explanations.

previousVersion.stem: To assess interference, compare an incongruent condition with:
options: An appropriate neutral or congruent control
previousVersion.explanation: A comparison condition helps isolate the cost associated with conflict.

units.title: Read a social structure
units.subtitle: Distinguish institutions, roles, and levels of explanation.

blocks.title: Move between levels
blocks.text: A micro-level explanation examines interactions among people. A macro-level explanation examines large institutions and social patterns. Both levels can address the same outcome with different units of analysis.

blocks.title: Identify a role
blocks.text: A status is a social position; a role is an expected pattern of behavior associated with that position. Role conflict involves incompatible demands across roles; role strain concerns competing demands within a role.

blocks.title: Compare perspectives
blocks.text: Functionalist accounts ask how parts contribute to social organization. Conflict approaches examine power and unequal resources. Symbolic interactionist accounts emphasize meanings developed through interaction. These are lenses for asking questions, not automatic proofs.

example.prompt: A student must attend an exam and work a scheduled shift at the same time. Is this role conflict or role strain?
example.reasoning: It is conflict between the student and employee roles. Competing expectations within a single role would instead illustrate role strain.

units.prediction: A student must attend an exam and work a scheduled shift at the same time. Is this role conflict or role strain? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: A social position such as student is a:
questions.explanation: Status is a social position. A role comprises expectations attached to a position, a norm is a shared rule, and a sanction is a response to behavior.

previousVersion.stem: A social position such as student is a:
previousVersion.explanation: Status names a social position; roles describe expectations associated with it.

questions.stem: Incompatible demands between employee and parent roles illustrate:
questions.explanation: Conflict between different roles, such as employee and parent, is role conflict. Role strain concerns demands within one role; role exit means leaving a role.

previousVersion.stem: Incompatible demands between employee and parent roles illustrate:
previousVersion.explanation: The demands come from different roles.

questions.stem: An approach emphasizing meanings in face-to-face interaction is:
options: Social exchange theory focused on costs and rewards
questions.explanation: Symbolic interactionism emphasizes meanings constructed and negotiated in interaction. Functionalism focuses on institutional functions; conflict theory emphasizes power and inequality; exchange accounts emphasize costs and rewards.

previousVersion.stem: An approach emphasizing meanings in face-to-face interaction is:
previousVersion.explanation: Symbolic interactionism studies socially developed meanings and interactions.

questions.stem: A study of nationwide educational institutions primarily uses which scale?
options: Micro: individual interpretations during a classroom exchange
Meso: relationships within one school organization
questions.explanation: A nationwide institutional pattern is a macro-level focus. Individual encounters are micro-level; a bounded organization is commonly examined at the meso level.

previousVersion.stem: A study of nationwide educational institutions primarily uses which scale?
previousVersion.explanation: Institutions and national patterns are macro-level units of analysis.

questions.stem: A teacher struggles to give individual feedback while grading a large class. Competing demands within this role illustrate:
options: Role conflict between unrelated social positions
questions.explanation: Competing demands within the teacher role illustrate role strain. No second distinct role, departure from teaching, or preparation for a future role is specified.

previousVersion.stem: A teacher struggles to give individual feedback while grading a large class. Competing demands within this role illustrate:
previousVersion.explanation: Both expectations arise within the teacher role.

questions.stem: An analysis asks who benefits from unequal resource distribution. It most closely reflects a:
options: Symbolic interactionist perspective on shared meanings
Social exchange analysis of a single interpersonal interaction
questions.explanation: Asking who benefits from unequal resource distribution emphasizes power and competing interests, characteristic of a conflict perspective. The other approaches emphasize meanings, functions, or individual exchanges.

previousVersion.stem: An analysis asks who benefits from unequal resource distribution. It most closely reflects a:
options: Claim that inequality has no structure
previousVersion.explanation: Conflict approaches focus on power and unequal resources.

units.title: Distinguish income, wealth, and mobility
units.subtitle: Read inequality without turning group patterns into individual certainty.

blocks.title: Separate stocks and flows
blocks.text: Income is money received over a period. Wealth is accumulated assets minus liabilities at a point in time. Similar current income can coexist with very different wealth.

blocks.title: Describe mobility
blocks.text: Intragenerational mobility occurs within a person’s life. Intergenerational mobility compares social position across generations. Structural mobility reflects broader economic or institutional changes rather than only individual movement.

blocks.title: Keep levels distinct
blocks.text: Socioeconomic measures can correlate with access, exposure, and health outcomes. An association does not identify a single mechanism or determine every individual outcome. Operational definitions and possible confounders matter.

example.prompt: Two households earn the same annual salary, but one owns substantial assets and the other has debt. Do they necessarily have equal wealth?
example.reasoning: No. Equal income flows do not imply equal net asset stocks. Measure assets and liabilities to compare wealth.

units.prediction: Two households earn the same annual salary, but one owns substantial assets and the other has debt. Do they necessarily have equal wealth? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Assets minus liabilities measure:
questions.explanation: Wealth is a stock of assets minus liabilities. Income is a flow over time, and gross assets omit the debt needed to calculate net worth.

previousVersion.stem: Assets minus liabilities measure:
previousVersion.explanation: Wealth is a stock of net assets.

questions.stem: Mobility between a parent’s and child’s social positions is:
options: Occupational change during a single lifetime
questions.explanation: Intergenerational mobility compares generations, such as parent and child. Intragenerational mobility tracks changes within one person’s lifetime.

previousVersion.stem: Mobility between a parent’s and child’s social positions is:
previousVersion.explanation: The comparison spans generations.

questions.stem: A survey finds a population association between socioeconomic status and health. Which conclusion is warranted about individual outcomes?
options: The association determines the outcome of each person in the group
The association establishes income as the sole cause of health differences
Individual outcomes can vary despite the population association
The association rules out individual exceptions when the sample is large
questions.explanation: A population-level association does not assign a certain outcome to every individual or establish a sole causal mechanism. Sample size can improve precision without removing individual variation.

previousVersion.stem: A population association between SES and health determines every individual outcome:
options: Only if the sample is large
previousVersion.explanation: A group-level association does not make each individual outcome certain.

questions.stem: A person moves from a low-paying to a higher-paying occupation during adulthood. This is:
options: Horizontal mobility between positions of equal socioeconomic standing
Structural mobility established solely by this individual move
questions.explanation: A change in a person’s own social position over adulthood is intragenerational mobility. Intergenerational comparison requires another generation, and one move alone does not establish a structural shift affecting an entire group.

previousVersion.stem: A person moves from a low-paying to a higher-paying occupation during adulthood. This is:
previousVersion.explanation: The change occurs within one person’s lifetime.

questions.stem: Equal salaries but unequal inherited assets demonstrate why researchers distinguish:
questions.explanation: Salary is income received over time, while inherited assets contribute to accumulated wealth. Equal salaries therefore do not imply equal net assets.

previousVersion.stem: Equal salaries but unequal inherited assets demonstrate why researchers distinguish:
previousVersion.explanation: Annual earnings and accumulated assets capture different resources.

questions.stem: An entire occupational sector expands and changes many workers’ positions. This can contribute to:
options: Exchange mobility within an unchanged distribution of positions
Horizontal mobility with unchanged socioeconomic standing
Individual mobility explained only by personal effort
questions.explanation: Expansion of a sector changes the distribution of available positions and can produce structural mobility. The pattern is not merely people swapping places within a fixed distribution.

previousVersion.stem: An entire occupational sector expands and changes many workers’ positions. This can contribute to:
previousVersion.explanation: Broader economic changes can shift opportunities across many people.

units.title: Interpret groups and populations
units.subtitle: Distinguish influence mechanisms and demographic measures.

blocks.title: Identify the social mechanism
blocks.text: Conformity involves adjusting behavior toward group norms. Obedience involves responding to an authority’s instruction. Social facilitation can improve a dominant, well-practiced response while impairing a difficult unfamiliar one.

blocks.title: Choose the denominator
blocks.text: A count is not a rate. Comparing births, deaths, or disease events across populations requires an appropriate population and time denominator. Population composition can affect crude comparisons.

blocks.title: Read social support carefully
blocks.text: Networks can provide emotional, informational, or practical support. Associations between network characteristics and health may reflect multiple pathways and selection effects. Avoid treating an observed association as a randomized intervention.

example.prompt: One city has twice as many events but four times as many residents over the same period. Is its per-person event rate higher?
example.reasoning: No. Its rate is half as large: twice the numerator divided by four times the denominator. Always inspect the population at risk and time period.

units.prediction: One city has twice as many events but four times as many residents over the same period. Is its per-person event rate higher? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: Changing behavior to match a group norm is commonly described as:
options: Obedience to a direct authority command
Compliance with a specific personal request
Social loafing during a collective task
questions.explanation: Conformity involves aligning with a group norm. Obedience emphasizes an authority’s command, compliance a request, and social loafing reduced individual effort in a group.

previousVersion.stem: Changing behavior to match a group norm is commonly described as:
previousVersion.explanation: Conformity concerns alignment with group norms or behavior.

questions.stem: Following an authority’s direct instruction most clearly illustrates:
options: Conformity to an unspoken peer norm
Compliance with a peer’s informal request
Internalization of a privately held belief
questions.explanation: Obedience is the clearest label for following a direct instruction from an authority. Peer norms, informal requests, and private belief change have different defining conditions.

previousVersion.stem: Following an authority’s direct instruction most clearly illustrates:
previousVersion.explanation: Obedience concerns responding to authority.

questions.stem: To compare event rates across cities, you need:
options: Event totals and city area, without a population denominator
Events, population at risk, and time period
Population sizes without event counts or a time window
Event counts and population sizes from unmatched time periods
questions.explanation: Rates require events, a relevant population-at-risk denominator, and a comparable time period. Raw counts, land area, or mismatched time windows can create misleading comparisons.

previousVersion.stem: To compare event rates across cities, you need:
options: Events, population at risk, and time period
previousVersion.explanation: Rates require an appropriate denominator and observation period.

questions.stem: A population doubles while events remain constant over the same period. Events per person:
questions.explanation: With events unchanged and the population doubled, the event-per-person ratio is halved. The time window is held fixed, so it does not introduce another scaling factor.

previousVersion.stem: A population doubles while events remain constant over the same period. Events per person:
previousVersion.explanation: The same numerator divided by twice the denominator gives half the rate.

questions.stem: An audience improves a practiced task but impairs an unfamiliar task. This fits:
options: Social loafing through reduced individual effort
Group polarization toward more extreme attitudes
Social facilitation of a dominant response
questions.explanation: An audience can strengthen the dominant response: helpful for a practiced task, harmful when that response is inappropriate for an unfamiliar task. Loafing, polarization, and deindividuation describe different group effects.

previousVersion.stem: An audience improves a practiced task but impairs an unfamiliar task. This fits:
options: Social facilitation of a dominant response
previousVersion.explanation: Audience effects can favor dominant responses, helping easy tasks and hurting difficult ones.

questions.stem: People with larger support networks report better health in a survey. This establishes:
options: That expanding a network necessarily improves a person’s health
That better health necessarily causes a larger network
An association requiring further causal analysis
That network size explains health independently of socioeconomic factors
questions.explanation: The survey establishes an association. Either direction of causation and confounding remain possible without additional design or analysis.

previousVersion.stem: People with larger support networks report better health in a survey. This establishes:
options: An association requiring further causal analysis
That networks alone cause all health differences
previousVersion.explanation: Observational associations leave selection and common causes to evaluate.

units.title: Interpret bands and controls
units.subtitle: Ask what molecule the assay detects.

blocks.title: Identify the target
blocks.text: A nucleic-acid gel separates fragments under specified conditions, often primarily by size. Western blotting detects proteins using antibodies. A signal’s interpretation depends on specificity and the experimental protocol.

blocks.title: Use the control
blocks.text: A loading control helps evaluate whether samples contain comparable loaded material, but its own stability must be justified. A missing target band can reflect low target abundance, technical failure, or an unsuitable assay.

blocks.title: Avoid overclaiming
blocks.text: Protein abundance and protein activity are different measurements. More band signal does not prove greater activity per molecule. A band at an unexpected size can motivate hypotheses about processing or modification, but needs supporting evidence.

example.prompt: A target band weakens and the loading-control band weakens by the same proportion. Does the target necessarily decline relative to loaded material?
example.reasoning: No. The pattern may reflect less loaded material. Normalize appropriately and verify that the control is stable under the treatment.

units.prediction: A target band weakens and the loading-control band weakens by the same proportion. Does the target necessarily decline relative to loaded material? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: A Western blot usually detects:
options: A DNA sequence recognized by a nucleic-acid probe
An RNA transcript recognized by a complementary probe
A protein recognized by an antibody
questions.explanation: Western blots use antibody recognition to detect protein targets. Nucleic-acid probes identify DNA or RNA in other assays, while turnover requires an activity measurement.

previousVersion.stem: A Western blot usually detects:
options: A protein recognized by an antibody
previousVersion.explanation: Western blotting uses antibody recognition of proteins.

questions.stem: A loading control helps assess:
options: The antibody’s exclusive specificity for the target
The biological effect caused by changing the target
questions.explanation: A suitable loading control helps assess sample-input comparability. It does not by itself establish antibody specificity, protein function, or causality for a phenotype.

previousVersion.stem: A loading control helps assess:
options: Catalytic activity directly in all cases
previousVersion.explanation: It supports loading comparison when the control itself is appropriate and stable.

questions.stem: For the same target, comparable loading, a specific antibody, and a validated linear detection range, a stronger Western blot band supports greater:
options: Detected abundance under the assay conditions
questions.explanation: Under these validated assay conditions, stronger target signal supports more detected protein. Saturation, changing antibody recognition, background, or unstable loading controls can undermine the comparison. Abundance still does not establish activity per molecule.

questions.stem: Both target and control intensities fall by half. Their ratio:
questions.explanation: Dividing half the target by half the control preserves the ratio.

questions.stem: An antibody intended to detect one target also reacts with several unrelated proteins. The main concern is assay:
questions.explanation: Unintended binding to multiple proteins threatens specificity, the ability to identify the intended target. Sensitivity, repeatability, and linear response address different assay properties.

previousVersion.stem: An antibody reacts with multiple proteins. The main concern is assay:
previousVersion.explanation: Cross-reactivity can make a signal ambiguous with respect to its intended target.

questions.stem: A protein is abundant but catalytically inactive. Which additional assay is needed to establish function?
options: Another Western blot of the same target
Measurement of the target gene’s copy number
questions.explanation: Function requires an assay of activity, such as product formation under defined conditions. Repeating abundance, transcript, or gene-copy measurements cannot establish catalytic activity.

previousVersion.stem: A protein is abundant but catalytically inactive. Which additional assay is needed to establish function?
previousVersion.explanation: Abundance alone does not demonstrate catalytic activity.

units.title: Turn absorbance into evidence
units.subtitle: Use a blank, a calibration, and a valid range.

blocks.title: Separate signal from background
blocks.text: A blank estimates background from solvent and reagents under the chosen protocol. Correcting for background helps isolate analyte-related signal. It does not eliminate all sources of error.

blocks.title: Use Beer–Lambert reasoning
blocks.text: Within a suitable range, A = εlc: absorbance is proportional to concentration and path length for a specified absorbing species and wavelength. Absorbance is logarithmic in transmitted-light fraction, A = −log10(T).

blocks.title: Check the range
blocks.text: A calibration curve relates known standards to measured signal. Extrapolation outside a validated range can fail, especially with scattering, chemical changes, or detector limitations. Dilution can bring a sample into range if accounted for afterward.

example.prompt: A sample diluted fourfold reads 2 concentration units on a valid calibration. What was the original concentration?
example.reasoning: The original concentration was 8 units, assuming dilution was performed correctly and the calibrated response applies to the diluted sample.

units.prediction: A sample diluted fourfold reads 2 concentration units on a valid calibration. What was the original concentration? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: A blank primarily estimates:
options: The calibration slope relating signal to analyte concentration
The analyte’s concentration without a calibration model
The dilution factor applied to the sample
questions.explanation: A suitable blank estimates signal from components other than the analyte, such as solvent and reagents. Calibration standards establish the response relationship; dilution is tracked separately.

previousVersion.stem: A blank primarily estimates:
previousVersion.explanation: A blank captures relevant background under the protocol.

questions.stem: At fixed ε and l within the valid range, doubling c should:
questions.explanation: At fixed molar absorptivity and path length in the linear range, doubling concentration doubles absorbance. Since T = 10^(-A), the transmitted fraction becomes its previous value squared; it does not double.

questions.stem: Transmittance T = 0.1 corresponds to absorbance:
questions.explanation: A transmitted fraction of 0.1 is 10⁻¹. Absorbance is −log10(T), so A = −(−1) = 1. Use the transmitted fraction, not a percentage of 10.

questions.stem: A fivefold-diluted sample measures 3 μM. Original concentration is:
questions.explanation: Multiply the measured diluted concentration by five.

questions.stem: An unknown exceeds the calibration range. A useful next step is to:
options: Extrapolate the calibration line beyond the validated range
Report the highest standard’s concentration as the unknown value
Subtract the blank again to bring the reading into range
Dilute into range and account for dilution
questions.explanation: Diluting into the validated range allows use of the calibration, followed by correction for the dilution factor. Extrapolation, clipping to a standard, or repeating blank subtraction does not establish the unknown concentration.

previousVersion.stem: An unknown exceeds the calibration range. A useful next step is to:
options: Dilute into range and account for dilution
previousVersion.explanation: A suitable dilution can allow a valid calibrated measurement.

questions.stem: Path length doubles while concentration and ε stay fixed. Predicted absorbance:
questions.explanation: Beer–Lambert absorbance is proportional to path length at fixed concentration and molar absorptivity. Doubling path length therefore doubles absorbance within the valid linear range.

previousVersion.stem: Path length doubles while concentration and ε stay fixed. Predicted absorbance:
previousVersion.explanation: Absorbance is proportional to optical path length in the valid model.
