units.title: Match evidence to a conclusion
units.subtitle: Use replication, uncertainty, and comparison groups.

blocks.title: Separate error types
blocks.text: Random error creates variability across measurements; systematic error biases a measurement in a consistent direction. More replicates can improve precision of an average but do not necessarily remove a shared calibration bias.

blocks.title: Identify the unit
blocks.text: Technical repeats of one biological sample are not independent biological replicates. The experimental unit is the independently treated unit. Confusing the two can exaggerate the amount of independent evidence.

blocks.title: Bound the inference
blocks.text: Statistical significance does not measure effect size or establish practical importance. A confidence interval expresses uncertainty under a model and procedure. Read the design, estimate, and uncertainty together before making a causal claim.

example.prompt: A researcher measures the same culture ten times after one treatment. Are there ten independent treated cultures?
example.reasoning: No. These are technical measurements of one biological unit. They can inform measurement variability but do not replace independent biological replication.

units.prediction: A researcher measures the same culture ten times after one treatment. Are there ten independent treated cultures? State your prediction and the principle you used before revealing the reasoning.

questions.stem: A miscalibrated scale adds the same offset repeatedly. This is:
questions.explanation: A repeatable calibration offset is systematic measurement error. Random variation fluctuates between measurements; neither sampling variation nor a biological treatment effect explains a constant instrument offset.

previousVersion.stem: A miscalibrated scale adds the same offset repeatedly. This is:
previousVersion.explanation: A persistent offset is a systematic measurement bias.

questions.stem: Ten measurements of one sample are primarily:
questions.explanation: Repeated readings of one sample are technical repeats. They estimate measurement repeatability but do not create new biological samples or independently assigned experimental units.

previousVersion.stem: Ten measurements of one sample are primarily:
previousVersion.explanation: Repeated measurements of one sample do not create independent biological units.

questions.stem: A study reports p < 0.01 but gives no effect estimate. Which conclusion about practical importance is justified?
options: A small p-value establishes that the effect is large
A small p-value establishes that the effect matters in practice
A small p-value establishes that bias is negligible
Practical importance cannot be determined from the p-value alone
questions.explanation: Statistical significance does not report effect magnitude, practical relevance, or freedom from bias. Evaluate the effect estimate, its uncertainty, study design, and the decision context.

previousVersion.stem: Statistical significance alone establishes a large practical effect:
previousVersion.explanation: Statistical evidence and effect magnitude are distinct considerations.

questions.stem: More repeats reduce variability of an average but preserve a calibration offset. Which problem remains?
options: Sampling error eliminated by the repeats
A treatment effect created by the offset
questions.explanation: Averaging can reduce random variability but does not remove a calibration offset. The remaining systematic bias should be addressed through calibration, not assumed to disappear with more repeats.

previousVersion.stem: More repeats reduce variability of an average but preserve a calibration offset. Which problem remains?
options: No measured uncertainty of any kind
previousVersion.explanation: Repeating the same biased method does not automatically remove its offset.

questions.stem: Treatment is randomized to entire classrooms. The independent treatment unit is the:
options: Individual student regardless of classroom assignment
Each repeated score from a student
Each question answered on the outcome test
questions.explanation: Randomization occurs at the classroom level, making classroom the treatment-assignment unit. Students and repeated scores within a classroom are not independent treatment assignments.

previousVersion.stem: Treatment is randomized to entire classrooms. The independent treatment unit is the:
previousVersion.explanation: The unit receiving independently assigned treatment determines the experimental unit.

questions.stem: Two studies report the same effect estimate but different uncertainty. A sound comparison should consider:
options: Only the study with the smaller p-value
Only the number of observations in each study
Only whether either interval crosses the null value
Both the estimate and its uncertainty
questions.explanation: Compare both effect size and uncertainty, alongside design and measurement context. A p-value, sample size, or null-crossing decision alone does not convey the whole comparison.

previousVersion.stem: Two studies report the same effect estimate but different uncertainty. A sound comparison should consider:
options: Whether the estimates use the same font
Both the estimate and its uncertainty
previousVersion.explanation: Precision and design affect how strongly an estimate supports an inference.
